THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
Pv JOSEPH HOCKING,
Author of "The Birthright," "Mistress Nancy Molesworth," "All Men are _Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," &c.
CIIAPTER XX V.

Share ttit brunt ot her other's anger, gave illtki joy untold. And ye he knew not wbat to do. He knew how loyal Lady Neville was to the faith of' her fathers, knew .how bitterly she would resent her daughter's desertion. Ile wished to save Alizon from words which he was sure would be spoken, longed to take to hintself everything which might wound her. And yet he reflected that he might help her by being near her; and he longed more than words could tell to shield her from'all pain. For himself he cared nothing. Since Alizon's declaration he felt that he could face anything. The thought of her love made impossibilities pose ible. Remembering the worde she had spoken, he felt strong enough to brave the anger of not only Lady Neville, but all the dignitaries of the Church as well. • _

"It is no use, Duncan," repeated Alizon, "I am going with you. I should never forgive myself if on the night of our—that is, if on this night of all others, I was afraid to stand by your side. You will let me come, won't you? I—l do so want to stay a little longer with you, you know!" The wilfulness and the winsomeness expressed in the same breath, conquered the young man. Like all other lovers he was but clay in the hands of the potter. He knew that now, as always, the will of the girl by his side would be his also, and that she, because she loved him, would, will for the best. _
They entered, side by side, the room in which Lady Neville sat awaiting her daughter.
CHAPTER XXVI.
HOW LADY NEVILLE RECEIVED THE NEWS.

Lady Neville looked jjp from the book she had been reading with a ?mile on her face as her daughter entered. Then, as she saw Duncan, the smile changed to a look of questioning. "Lady 'lngram has just gone," she said, quietly, "and I was wondering how long you would be. How are you, Mr. Rutland? It was a very imposing ceremony at St. Peter's to-day, wasn't it ? " "Very," replied Duncan. "Did you get near his Holiness ? " "Oh, yes, thank you. He stopped for a minute close to where I stood." "Alt, that is well. There was such a crowd that I was afraid you would be unable to obtain a sight of him. He is a wonderful man, isn't he? Fancy such strength at ninety. He must be under an egpecial Providence; doubtless he is. Don't you think so ? "
"1 trust we are all under an especial Providence," replied Rutland, "but he is a very wonderful old man, very wonderful. Thank you, very much for giving me the opportunity of seeing him. "
"Oh, that is all right. I hope it may continue to be a source of satisfaction to you. Alizon, you look pale and tired. I think you had better retire."
"Lady Neville, "said Rutland, "you must wonder why I have taken the liberty of calling to-night. If you will allow me, I will tell you in a few words."
"By all means." She looked into his face as though she expectad a pleasant communication. "1 have come to tell you that I love your daughter, and to ask your consent for her to become my wife."
Lady geville looked at him with speechless astonishment.
"I do not quite understand you, I am afraid,." she said presently. "I love Alizon," he repeated, simply. "I have loved her for nearly a year now." _
"You love Alison! "- " Yes, your ladyship." "And—and you have told her this ? 7 "Yes, I have told her." "And she? You, Alison? "
"She has made me a happy man, perhaps the happiest man in the world." His voice was husky, and he spoke quietly, almost reverently. "When did she tell you this ? "
"To-night." , .Lady Neville rose to her feet, her eyes flashed with anger. Rutland irould not have been sur- prised if she had bidden him to leave the room.
"Alizon;" se said presently, "will you leave us. Mr. Rutland and I had better speak of this matter alone."
"I would rather not, mother."
"What do. you mean ? "

"Only thi;," Alizon's face was very pale, and her lips were tremulous, but she mastered herself. and spoke quietly. "You will accuse Duncan of things which he will not deny, and which will not be true; you will say what you ought not to say to him—and—and I wish to stay:"

Lady Neville was evidently very angry. She toyed impatiently with some trifles on the table by her side, and seemed in doubt as to what she should say next. "Do you think you have acted honourably with me. Mr. Rutland ? " she asked presently. , Rutland was silent; he was afraid at that moment that he ought to have told Lady Neville of his love months before.

"Is—is this your return for the—the kindness I —I have tried to shew you ? " she continued. Had she not been very angry she would never have spoken in this fashion; but under the circum- stances she could barely govern her words. "Perhaps I ought to have spoken to you before," replied Rutland. "Possibly I ought to have told you on the night I discovered my love. But in those days it seemed pure madness on my part to lift my eyes to Alizon. ' "It is still," replied her ladyship. "That, of course, must be understood."

"I know it, and yet I cannot help it," was Ru ti and ' s response. "Will you tell me the history of this foolish- ness?" said her ladyship presently. "Perhaps when I know that I can shew you how—how utterly impossible it is for me to countenance the affair."

"I am afraid its history is my own history after I came to Lynford," replied Duncan. "You know how I was thrown into contact with Alizon, and— and I could not help loving her." The young fellow said this so humbly, yet so manfully, that for a moment her ladyship felt less bitterly towards him. Perhaps she thought of the time when her own heart first warmed towards Sir Charles Neville, and the memory of that time made her young again. "And -how long is it since you first spoke to Alizon about this ?" she asked. "It is some months ago." "And why did you not tell me?" asked Lady Neville, turning towards her daughter. "Because," and Alizon spoke steadily, "because I hoped then that Duncan's love was only a passing fancy. It was altogether strange to me, and it seemed so impossible that I could not entertain it seriously. Besides, I did not tell you because I thought if you knew you would forbid his coming to the Priory." "Certainly I should, and what then?" Alizun was silent; she did not know how to express her thoughts. Lady Neville, however, interpreted her silence rightly, and for a moment the position staggered her. Here was surely a strange outcome to her plans for the young minister's conversion. How blind she had been never to have thought of this contingency! She remembered that she had invited Rutland to the Priory, had remonstrated with him when he failed to take advantage of her invitations. "Tell me the whole truth," she said, angrily. "Was it at your wish that my daughter did not tell Me of your madness?" "It was not," cried Alizon. "I —I thought he would forget it, and it was I who suggested that his words should be regarded as not spoken. Duncan never hinted at such a thing." The girl seemed to take a pride in taking all possible blame on herself, it was for this reason that she had insisted on taking her place by his side during the interview. "But did you give no encouragement when ,he first spoke ? " "No," said Duncan, "none at all. She told me that even if she could ever care for me she would destroy all possibility of affection while I remained a Protestant."

A sneer curled her ladyship's lips. She thought she saw how matters stood, and she despised the young minister accordingly. Still, it might he for the best; the man who could change his faith in order to win a girl would not be difficult to deal , with. Some sort of compromise could be effected somehow. Besides, if be professed conversion to the Catholic faith he would be under the discipline of the Church. The whole affair was terribly disappointing, but it might be all for the best. Immediately she became more cool and collected she was able to talk with more deliberation.
"Well, and so I suppose you began to be drawn to our faith? "

There was a touch of scorn in her voice, for she was a high-smiled woman. Faith to her was a, sacred thing, and she could not 'conceive how any- one could associate base considerations with matters of religions. "No, I do not know that I was drawn to it,* replied Rutland, "but I loved Alizon so much that

MY DEAR NELLIE, A hat which I liked immensely was of felt, and has a crown embroidered with steel beads and sequins, with a couple of natural-coloured quills stuck through it. A quilling of white sill; under the brim is very pretty. A hat of velvet, with ostrich tips, and a twist of white silk under the turned-up brim, adorned with two rows of steel ornamentation, and terminated by a tasteful rosette at either end. Among others, there is a brown felt hat, trimmed ,with feather pom-poms, two natural brown and two azure-blue, and velvet and silk. A felt hat, with corded brim, had silk and velvet bows on it, and a couple of mauve- grey quill. A very pretty hat, of stylish shape, was in black panne, with a tucked velvet crown and a tucked panne brim. The trimming is draped with handsome white lace across the front, .and on the left are two large quills, while on the right there are two loops of black ribbed velvet, with a knot in the centre.

There are a number of very excellent costumes going around and you should have no difficulty in selecting one to your taste. A costume which I have fancied is made of fine cloth or cashmere. The foundation is of silk, with a shaped flounce of cloth at the bottom, and another of printed velveteen above it; the overskirt is stitched at the bottom to match the bottom flounce. The cross- cver bodice has large revers and turned-back cuffs ,of velveteen, and a waistband of velvet and velveteen to match; the sleeves from the elbow to the wrist are of lace over white satin, and a -chemisette of tucked white chiffon is worn at the throat. This design is suitable for any kind of printed velveteen or fancy silk, and it could be carried out in plain and fancy woollen materials of the same colour. Dresses made of two distinct stuffs will be very fashionable this autumn, so I am informed on very good authority.

In a neat travelling dress which I have seen in a purplish tone of heather-mixture, the bands of trimming are merely rows of machine stitching which pass round the skirt, down the centre, and round the hem. The little coat fits closely to the figure, opening slightly in front to show a cream- coloured muslin blouse and a black crepe-de-chine tie, the ends of which are caught into gilt ferrets. {The scallopped revers are faced with -pale mauve 'panne, stitched down upon the tweed. The hat has no trimming that could be spoiled by weather. Who small buttoms that appear on the bodice are merely for ornament, not for use. The sleeves are of the plainest and simplest make.

The wooden heels with which the cheaper kind ,of shoe is now generally furnished break down very quickly when some hours a day are spent in walking. These heels are very much lighter than those made of leather, and are for that reason verj popular, but nothing gives a shabbier look to the traveller than the shoe that is worn down at heel. For this season it is better to choose a low, leather heel than a high wooden one. The latter thr3ws the foot out of its natural poise, and is conse- quently more fatiguing to the wearer than a low heel. The fault of most shoes is that they are cut too narrow across the sole. This makes the uppers. wear out very quickly at the sides, where they are pressed down upon the ground to afford the foot sufficient room. The days are gone when size four was the average wear of English-women. Increase in height and the outdoor life led by girls have had their influence upon the foot, and sizes six and seven are now the average. Shoemakers tell of girls for whom sizes eight and nine, and even 10, are made. They affirm that bicycling has greatly developed the feet of Englishwomen. Your loving

div.head: AFTERWARDS.
div.p: AFTERWARDS.

Alizon Neville's secret was out at last, she had told Ruth,nd more than he had dared to hope for. "Do you mean hat?t " he cried, "do you mean that you—you wish me to stay, that you—you—-" They were in the square alone beneath the olive trees, no prying eyes were near, no listening ears everheard the girl's confession. • Duncun caught her hands in his, and looked into her eyes. He had forgotten all about the differ- ences in their faith, forgotten that. she had been reared in a world 'different from his own. They were man and maid together, and they loved each other. At that moment neither realised what must inevitably lie before them, or even if they did, it did not blight their happiness. They feared nothing; anger, threats, persecution, were as nothing. In many respects the supreme moment of their lives had come, and everything save their love was ,forgotten. For let who will say other- wise, there is nothing, limnanly speaking, so wondrous, or so great, as the joy of the man who knows that the love of his heart is returned. A. few minutes before Duncan's sky was black, he saw nothing before him but a life of loneliness and disappointment. His life's work would have to be done under the shadow of unfulfilled desires, and the cravings of his heart would never be satisfied. Now all was changed. Alizon loved him, and in that knowledge the. world became new. "You are sure?" he said presently, "you are quite sure? Tell me quickly. Your answer is everything to me." "Yes," she said, and in her voice was a laugh and a sob. "I —I could not help it," she added. A second later their lips met in their first kiss, and: Duncan Rutland and Alizon Neville were betrothed.

For a time they were oblivious to everything save their own happiness. Had they been some village lad and lass wandering in a country lane, their lore-making could not have been more simple, they could not have cared lees for the eyes of the world. She was only a girl of twenty, and he a few years older. They forgot to be coventional as they whispered to each other the words that trans- formed the cold dark night into a June morning. Realities c,rne back to them presently, however. The fact of their difference of faith came rushing back to the young man's memory. He remembered that she was a Catholic, and,that she :had regarded him as an enemy to the truth. "And you will be my wife, Alizori? " "Yes, if you will have me." "The wife of a poor Protestant minister?" "You know."
But he could not realise it, he could not under- stand tho change which had come over her. "You will forgive my being what you call a heretic? " "You are not a heretic." "Alizon!"

"Oh, I have been wanting to tell you for days past, only I dared not. It would seem as though —but you know." "What do you mean, Alizon ? Surely, surely— has God given you light?" "It was no use. I held on as long as I could. Before I knew you I did not think, I simply accepted. I believed that to doubt was sin. I said in my heart that the greatest thinkers of the world had settled all these matters. That the Church was infallible, and that those who were outside its pale were outside salvation. I—l held to this while you were in Lynford, and I came here hoping and believing that you would be converted. But, Duncan, sin or no sin, I cannot believe longer." "Not in your Church?"

"No, s impossible to me. I—l, oh, I cannot tell you all I've gone through since I have been here. I dared not speak to anyone about it. I was afraid even to tell my mother. You see—l am afraid even you cannot understand." "Yes, I think can. But tell me, tell me everything."

"I don't know why, but I've been so dis- appointed since I came to Rome. The Church is not what I expected. Its ideals are so peor com- parzil with what I hoped. It seemed to resolve everything into a system, and to ,upport thi4 syst6m at•whatever cost. And this, while I could not argue about it, fell short of my longings. But that which really made me begin to doubt was that —that Bambino." "Yes, I understand." "Oh, I cannot explaia it, The priests and the nurse believed so implicitli; without any tangible evidence, :just as they seemed to believe everything else. And then that night, after mother had fallen asleep, and you had left . us, I went into the drawing-room, and that priest, Brother Francis, was lying on a sofa asleep. In spite of my anxiety, I almost laughed. And then I saw a New Testa- ment lying on a table.. As you know it is a for- bidden book to Catholics. That is, no Catholi is allowed to read it except under the supervision of the priest. I looked at it, end saw that it belonged to .011."

"Yee, I remember." "Well, I read for hours. Perhaps you have wondered where the book was ? " "I thought I had lost it." "I have had it ever since. I've read it throuzh time after time, praying for help and light. Oh, it is a wonderful book, and no one can realise what a revelation it has been to me."

"And that is.all ?" "It is all that can be put into words, but I think you can understand." That was the happiest night of Duncan Rutland's life. All, and more than he had ever hoped for had come to pass, the impossible had heen realised. The fair girl who walked by his Side had promised to be his wife.
"I must go and tell your mother, Alizon," he said presently. "Yes—and—and you will not go to Naples to- morrow ? "

"Not unless you will go with me." The girl laughed a happy laugh. They walked back towards the hotel together, along the Via della Quattra Fontane, and down the steps past the tablet to the memory of Keats, into the Piazza di Spagna. " The square was almost empty, and a great silence seemed to rest on the city. You remember the night we walked here together ? " said Rutland. "Yes, I remember." "You have told your mother nothing ? " "No, nothing. I have not dared." "She will be very angry, will she not ? " • "Duncan, you must help me. The Nevilles have been Catholics for hundreds of years, and mother is an implicit believer. Oh, lam afraid to think of what she will say." "We Nvi 11 know to-night. I cannot bear the suppense." "You are not afraid, are you?" Alizon asked the question with a little laugh. ; "Not now," said the young fellow, looking at her with eager eyes. "Because—because, there will not only be mother, but Father Sheen, and Father Ritzoom, and—and all the rest." -
"I was not afraid of either of them when you were against me, Alizon—now I am afraid of nothing."
A feCw. seconds later they reached the hotel.,
- "Jam going straight to my room, Duncan," said Alizon. "I expect Lady Ingram will have left before now. Mother will be waiting for me.", _

"Will you not speak to her to-night?" "I-1 don't know. lam such a coward." "You a coward, ?" "Yes. If I were not I should go with you to— to speak to incther. Would you rather I did?" "Not if it would pain you. \ They walked along the corridor together towards Lady/Neville's rooms. "Good-night, Alizon." Alizon was silent.
"Won't you say ,good-night to me ? " "Noe yet,"
"I won't be a coward, Duncan; I will go with you.." "No, -don't. Your mother's anger will have spent itself after a little while, and—and I will take all the blame."

"Please don't help me to be a coward, Duncan," said the girl. "No, no, I roust go with you." There was such a note of determination in her voice that he could not resist her ; besides, the fact that she desired to stand by his sine, and to

div.p: .1. said .1. Iv•..suld Ontuy e I.•‘Litilid again, Mal I would read Catholic. books, and understand Catholic arguments." "Yes, well." .
"As you know, I did not viAit the Priory for months. I dared not, I—l was not strong enough. I tried to destroy my love or Alizon, but I could not."

"No, I suppose not." Lady Neville felt sure she knew what was conning, and began to form plena whereby she could deal with the whole business. - "I need not say what .I endured. I tried to ne faithful to my Church. 1 tried to do my duty cll. Then I was taken ill."

At that moment Lady Neville felt that perhaps his mental struggle was real. The doctor had declared that the young minister had nearly killed himself by overwork and anxiety. Besides, hie voice had a: ring of truth. Doubtless, then, he was telling what had actually taken place, and thus hie conversion was real. It was as she had hoped, with the exception of his madness in loving Alizon. The case would be difficult to deal with, still, it could be dealt with. She wished that Ritzoom were in Rome, he would be able to advise with her. Well, and why not? A telegram would reach him in a few hours, and in three days he could be in Rome, meanwhile the matter could be left in abeyance.

"Yes; you were taken ill," said her-ladyship, "but you recovered. What then ? " "I reflected that I had never seen Romanism at its headquarters." said Rutland. "That although books had failed to convince me the sight of Rome, the home of the Vatican, and the centre of the system, would do so; for—for lam afraid I wanted to be converted. You see I loved—" _

"Yes, yes. Well, you came to Rome. And I suppose the work of the Church, her services, her history, and a sight of the Holy Father, did con- vince you ? " "No," replied Rutland, quietly, "no, they dt,' not convince me."

"What, do you mean then—that--" "I am stiii a Protestant, Lady Neville. lam more convinced in my opinion than ever." Lady Neville was staggered. Her castle of cards had fallen to the ground; with one blow all her plans were destroyed. "Then how dare you as a Protestant, as a heretic, dare to speak to my daughter again ? " she asked, angrily. "I trusted you as a gentleman. For that reason I consented to her accompanying you on some of your journeys. Is this your idea of acting as a man of honour ? "

Alizon opened her lips to speak, but Rutland stopped her. "I "lid not betray your trust," replied the young man. "Ae you know, Father Matthew accom- panied us in all our journeys, and neither by word nor sign did I act other than ae'an acquaintance to whom you had been kind." "Then to what circumstances do I owe the honour of this visit to night? "it was my fault,"' said Alizon, proudly. "I will speak," this to Duncan, who tried to answer Lady Neville 's question. "This morning, after our visit to the Sistine Chapel, he asked me to grant him an interview; knowing that you would be engaged with Lady Ingram, I told him that I would give it him to-night." _ . .

"I begin to see," said Lady Neville. "But may I ask the subject of discussion ? " "Ho told trke that he was going to Naples to- morrow," cried Alizon, excitedly. "He told me that—that he dared not, that is, he could not be in my society any longer." "It was my fault," cried Rutland. "I had tried to accept your faith, but I could not. I remem- bered that Alizon had told me that even if she felt any love for a Protestant she should feel it her duty to destroy it, and so I gave up all hope of ever winning her. And—and I could not bear being in her company, because I was consumed with a hopeless love, so I made up my mind to go to Naples. I know lewas wrong—that is, perhaps I ought to have gone away without speaking to ber, but I could not help it. So I—l told her that I muit remain a Protestant because—because Romanism seemed a string of fables, and that I must never see her again."

Rutland got out iThis speech stammeringly, and with great difficulty. He scarce knew what ho was saying, but in his heart was a great desire to take all blame upon himself. In his excitement, how- ever, he Uttered words which had better be left unsaid.

"I see," said Lady Neville, "you told Alizon that you must bid her good-bye for ever. Very proper and very romantic. But why do you come here? Why this mad confession and this more than mad request? Why have you not gone to Naples? " "Because I asked him not to go," cried Alizon. Her face was very pale, but her eyes burnt brightly "It was not his fault," she said proudly. a/ asked him to stay because I could not help it. He loved me, and has loved me for a long time, and I I love him, and I could not bear for him to go away." "Alizon I " cried Lady Neville, -sternly. "Oh, lam grieved to cause you pain, cried the girl, "and, 0 mother, I don't love you the less; but surely you can understand, surely you can feel for me. I cannot help it." For a moment Lady Neville's eyes grew soft, and she seemed like yielding to the pleading of her only child, but only for a moment. Anger and disappointment stee_ed her heart again and she spoke almost harshly. Besides, she (lid not know the whole,of the truth yet. What she had heard was but the preamble of what to her was almost as cruel as death itself. "No, I cannot understand," she said, bitterly. "How can I understand? Can you not see the madness of your request, the mocicery of .your position? How can you love a man who does not belong to your station in life, and who is—but why need I repeat it all You feel this, Mr. Rutland, you can underctand the impossibility of—of every- thing you ask ? " "No," cried Rutland. "I know I am your inferior in worldly position. Ido not belong to a great historical family; but—but God has mile us fit for each other. And—and I love her like my own life!"
"Love!" sneered Lady Neville. "Yes, I love her," cried Duncan. "I do not profess any other worthiness than this. She is all the world to me. I know lam a poor man, but —I am not a clown."

There was a touch of pride in his tones.' Alizon's love had made him bold, besides, he knew that intellectually he was Lady Neville's equal, and he prided himself upon being a gentleman. Perhaps her ladyship felt this as she looked at him. True, he did not belong to any of the families who might claim to be her equal, and he had not the bearing of a society man, but he looked what he was, a manly man. He had thrown aside his overcoat, and stood in evening dress by Alizon's side. Thera was nothing small nor weak about him. Both face and form were well moulded. His eyes shone clear and bright, and his words, though spoken under the influence of a great excitement, were those of a man of feeling— a man with the instincts of a gentleman. "I do not say you are a clown, Mr. Rutland,* she said, quietly. "But what you ask is impossible, impossible!" "Why?" asked Rutland. "There are many reasons why, any one of which would be sufficiently strong to keep me from grant- ing my consent. But I will give one, the one you have felt yourself. You are a Protestant."

"Yes, I am a Protestant," replied Rutland, quietly, "but I am sincere in my faith." "Yes, but Alizln is a Catholic, and white respect you personally—that is, I have respected you in the past—l could never consent for Alizon to .marry a—that is, a man of different faith." _ _
"But, hut---" stammered Rutland, and then he stopped. He knew that the revelation which hung upon his lips would be harder to bear, even than the confession of Alizon's lore for him.
He tried to speak again, but before his words formulated themselves into a sentence, Alizon fell on her knees at her mother's feet.
"Mother, mother!" she sobbed, "forgive me, but I have been obliged to give up my old faith!"

The Mayor (Alderman Roberts) presided at the Monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. There wrre also present :—Alderman Sutton, Couceillors Monks, Plumpton, Smethurst, Rogers, John Bvans,:Jaires Evans, S Davies, Baird. Forshaw, Edison, A Jelley, A J Jolley, 'finnion,J Shaw Green, L Greening, VY_Bkinson, F R Roberts, John Rs4berts, Peacock, with messrs J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Stanley Wilson (deputy town e!erk), Dr Gornall (medical officer), .J airhurst (bwough trt asurer).J De 3 s (sanitary engineer), Longdin (surveyor), J Sutcliffe (deputy surveyor), W 8 Haddock (gas engineer). The Late Councillor Lee. A resolution expressing regret at the death of Coun- tißor Lee was passed on the motion of the Mayor. The Maxim also spoke of the lcs3 Councilor Shillcgck had B.:stained in the death of his wife. It.was only due to him to express to him in an informal way their sense of the bereavement he was suffering from at the present time. Councillor Shillcok was a genial colleague. He Acted in a very straightforward manner;and had gained The respec.t of every member of the Corporation and:they deeply sympathhed with him in his present sorrow. (Rear, bear.) Finance and Estate Committee. £59,056 for Street Improvements. £9O for the Borough Auditors.

At a meeting of the above com—nlittee held on the 13th ugust, it was resolved that the Town Clerk be Instructed to apply to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of £59,055 for street kaprovement purposes. Proposed Widening of the Road at Arpley Station and Warrington Bridge. At a meeting of the General Purpuees Committee, the I following letter from the London and North-Western Railway Uompanv was read Euston Station, Lon- don, Augusto;h,looo. Dear sir.—Proposed widening o Iroad in front of station, Arnley, Warrington:: With reference to my letter of the 24th May last, the pmsposal Iby the Corporation to widen the private road of the Railwa,pCompany for the benefit of the parishioners has caused the whole circumstances connected with the road in question to be looked into, and it is now euggested that if the road were clo:ed entirely to the public by gates at each end, and only used in connection with rail- way business the necessity for improving the road would not arise, and not only that, but the Railway Company would be caved from a•very considerable sum annually in maintenance. From inquiries.' have made I gather that a very large preportioo of the traffic on the road has nothing whatever to do with the company's business or access ta the station. 'Before making any report to my directors upon the subject I should be glad tofknow if the Corporation look with favour on the closing of the road in ttle manner suggested by me, or would such a course create any considerable inconvenience to the users ofrthe road other than those going to and from the station.-4 am, dear sir, yours truly, E. MACKIE." It was resolved: That the TownqClerk info:m the coin any that the closing of the road as proposed would be a serious public inconvenience_ It was further resolved : That Mr. J. a man wno would rain benave nonouraniy ana reconcile duty with inclination. Impartial out- siders must decide according to their several notions of conduct whether it was or was not to Philip Pros,sley's credit. that he remained silent. His own notion was quite clearly that to play Mist Bob false would ho the act of a cad; hi casuistical powers were slender, and as he knew not what to say, he' said nothing. Lily Meade, after a moment, relieved him from further embarrassment by making swiftly for the door.
"I wonder," he murmured lugubriously, after it had closed behind her, "whether she under- stands?"

If she did not, there was somebody else in the house who was more ready of comprehension— somebody who, having been made the recipient of a confidential communication by the irate Lord Pennington, kept her eves open during dinner and arrived at certain conclusions. Hardly had Lily Meade retired to her bedroom when a brisk knock was followed by the entrance of Miss Gisborne, who, without wasting time upon intioductory remarks, said: "So you are off, with the new love, I hear. But you mustn't expect to be on with the old °fie again, you 'know." "I have never expected anything of the sort," the girl declared, colouring vividly. "4.11, that's all right, because I don't, as at present advised, see why I should surrender him to you. Beall po3sidc;te3 ! I stuck to him when he was poor and in misery, whereas. you turned your back upon him, remember." Lily shook her head. "It is not true that I turned my back upon him. I thought he wished for his liberty, and I gave it to him, but I do not for one moment complain of the use that he made of it, nor do I at all wonder at his caring more for you than he does for me." "H'm! you would wonder a good deal if you really believed that he did, I suspect. lam an ugly old maid, and you are—what your looking- glass tells you that you are; it stands to reason that you can give me stones and a beating in any contest of that nature. The only thing is that Philip Crossley needs a wife who hilts strength of mind enough to keep him straight, otherwise it won't take him long to run through a second fortune. Now, I venture to flatter myself that I shall be such a wife. Do you think you would be ? " _
"I don't know; perhaps not. What does it matter, since there is no question of my being tried?"

"Oh, it doesn't matter in that sense. What I want to point out is that I am not really as selfish as I may appear to you to be, and that in Philip's own interest he had much better marry me than you. Frankly now, could you, if you were put to it, restrain him from gambling ? " In her heart of hearts Lily thought that she could, but she replied, heroically and evasively: "I daresay you are right." "I am always right," Miss Bob returned, laughing; "it is a way I have. I was right, for instance, in surmising that you and he unbosomed yotoselves when you were in the library ,together before dinner; and I believe I am right in taking it for granted that your confabulation was free from any hint of treachery to the absent." "Yes, you are right there, you are indeed!" cried the girl eagerly. "I am glad of it.. That shews that you are decent people in your way, though it can't be said to slif,w that you would have proved.a success as husband and wife. Good-night." it was on the following day that Missel Thrush won the Leger with plenty to spare, thereby rejoicing the bookmakers and putting all the tipsters to confusion. His fortunate owner, who, after leading the horse in, was warmly con- gratulated by friends of both sexes, acknowledged their kindness, it was thought, sompwhat "Oh, the wretch happened to be in the humour," he said. And within himself he could not help ejaculating "al only the wretch had happened to be in the humour last June!"

How differeat, in that case, would have been .11r. Philip Crossley's actual position! By winning the Hardwicke Stakes he might have held on until now. 'Lily would still have been his; some portion, if xot the whole, of his uncle's money would surely have come to him, and that old dream of waking the turf a paying business need not,. perhaps, have been abandoned. But what use wfts there in lamenting the irrevocable? His business was to put a good face upon matters as they stood, and with such skill did he acquit him- self of that task that Miss Gisborne, when he encountepmd her between the paddock and the stand, excl ed-:

"You look as cheerful as if the stewards had been incifing you to account for your horse's in- and-outrunning! I.hope they haven't ? " Philip laughed rather ruefully. "I hope they -,voiet," he answered, "for notWng is more certain than tkEt I can't account for it. All I can tell the stewards or anybody else about the beast is that helms a nasty, perverse disposition." "ThK's one spirit in whieli to accept victory. I suppese your grievance is that you didn't back him ? "

"Oh, 'I did back him for a hundred, at starting price, 2 backinc, him signaled." Miss Bob, who had many masculine tricks, stood still, with her feet wide apart. placed her hands ~upon her hips and whistled *ith great solemnity. "It •-•G I gnifiis prodigiously!" she cried. "That you sliculd have backed any horse to win any- thing signitles, from my point of view, just about as lunch as it is possible to signify." She ,ought not to bar been astonished, con- sidering that Philip had elaterecl the ring and made his bet under her very eyes; yet she wore an air of downright consternation. "Have you forgotten," she asked, "that the one condition upon which I promised to marry you was that gou were to give up betting?" "I-remember your saying something of the sort. I doiet, remember making any promise," the young man answered.

"Nevertheless you did promise, and lam a woman of my word. What is to be done? If you forget:ence, you may forget again. I can't over- look elicit a warning as this without being false to the principles of a lifetime." Was•ever a more tempting way of escape offered to ono-who stood in sore need of loopholes? For an instant, but only for an instant, Philip hesitated. Then, since he was, after all, a gentle- man, ho cast temptation behind him and said: "nna-awfully sorry, Bob; I really didn't know I had:broken my word. But I'll tell you what I'll do, /11 promise you upon my honour never to have anotheiaket as long as I live. Will that satisfy you "Yes'," replied Miss Bob slowly and deliberately, "that Will satisfy me. It is distinctly understood, then, that you are bound in honour never—never under :any imaginable circumstances—to bet again ?" Phiti,p nodded. "Yes, that is the under- standinc" "Thank you very much. That being so, I feel that my mission is accomplished, and that I may remain tsvith a quiet conscience in the estate of indeponSeLt spinsterhood which I so greatly prefer to wedlock."

"Eh? "That you may do what?" "That may hand you over, with my blessing and my hest wishes, to Lily Meade, who does not appreciate the privileges of independence. My dear boy, cre you under the impression that engaged myself to marry you for the sake of your beaux yese You are, are you? Well, disabuse your mind .61 that flattering but slightly ridiculous idea. lam sincerely attached to you, it is true, And I hope we shall always be the best of friends; but it isn't at my time of life that one falls in love, like a,school-girl, with one's juniors. I iike you, I sways have liked you, well enough to faa anxious to save you from yourself by any mailable meats, and there was a moment when eapousing you seemed to be the only method open to ; but thasituation has changed since then. 1-011 have money enough to live upon in comfort now, and I have your word of honour, upon which I implicitly rely, that you won't squander it. I am fairly entitled, it seems to me, to consult my own wishes and retire. in Miss Lily's favour."
"Bb," gasped Philip, "do you really mean what pion say ? " "Do "returned Miss Bob, "look like a liar ? "

Her frank, good-humoured countenance certainly bore no appearance a belonging to a member of that ignoble class, yet it may be feared that, if there be a recording angel whose function it is to note down our misdeeds, she did not escape his vigilance. Whether we deserve, and receive, a black mark for sheer stupidity or not, who can tell? Let us hope that we do not, and that Philip and Lily Crossley, now happily united in holy matrimony, are held blameless in that they impute no blame to themselves.

Lord Pennington is pleased to proclaim aloud to all and sundry that he regards himself as having had a deuced lucky escape. As for Miss Bob, it must be obvious to everybody that her satisfaction with a union which she voluntarily brought about is genuine. Philip still owns a modest stud. It is a pity, he sometimes thinks, that he should be

preclunea, as an nonooraoie man, trom occasionally putting a trZe on dead Certainties; but, since the dead certainties do not invariably come off, theret is, perliays, no need to compassionate him very, profoundly on that account. [Tun END.]
ASTONISHING EXPERIENCE OF A MANCHESTER MAN.

The great British public rrais nothing with so MUCh avidity as the particulars of some wonderful escape from the jaws of aeatb, and a case—a remarkably case—in point has 1 oen unearthed by a repor:er of the "Buxton Advertiser "and " High Peak News.' In the first week of July the reporter learned that a young man had come final his home in Manchester to spend a week or two among the brerzy uplands of Derbyshire, and the curiosity of the reporter having been aroused respecting the adventures of this young fellow, be prrzeeded on July 23rd to the out-of-the-world village of Chelmorton, five miles from Buxton,to satisfy himself if the informa- tion given him mild be suttAanZiated. Outside a neat cJttage he met the object of his visit, ard was received in the most courteous manner imagin- able. In a few moments the reporter was busy making the following notes of an extraordinary story.

"My cam( W. H. Milborce, and my home is No. 1, Duke-street. Rusholme, Manchester. lam an insurance pgent, or was, when I was able to attend to business. For the last five year., more or lesq. I have been a great sufferer from sick-headaches. Various doctors were consultttd, and pronounced that I had Bright's disease,but of course I did not think so. Last D,cember I was taken much worse and put to bcd, and stayed there for twelve weeks. I was then living at Within- ton. After that I went into the Royal Hospital. at: Salford, and was there ten weeks, but whLn I was discharged from there I was no better." '6 What did you do next ?'' "I went to Southport Convalcscent Hospital for five weeks without deriving any benefit, and you may guess all this proved a heavy xpense for me. I have not earned one penny the last nine months."

"And yet you are looking very well and strong now!" "Yes, and I feel well. I saw an advertisement in a local paper, and I immediat?ly wrote to Dr. Williams' Medicine Company. Londcn, who sent me a letter in reply advising me to try Dr Willi4ma's pink pills for pale people. I procured a box in Manchester. After taking half a box I felt relieved, and by the time the box was! empty I felt very much better. I got anoth*r box, and hive continued to take them regularly, and I have F:radually improved during the whole time I was taking them. At the end of the fourth box I felt so much better that I now think I shall soon be able to start work again. I came out to Chelmorton a month ago." "The symptoms you sulZereu from were 9" " Heavy sickness, and it was no ordinary headache I suffered from; it was one of the severest kinds of sick- ness known. I was utterly exhausted at the least exer- tion, and had no heart for anything. I thought many times that I should never be well again, but there was no doubt as te the wonderful improvement that took place when I commenced Dr. Wiliams's pink pills." "Had you taken a lot of medicine before commencing with the pills 9" "Yes, but I have declined t 3 take any since. The doctors who attended me both at Manchester and at Salford said my sickness was of a very serious nature— Brigit's disease." "You has,- gradually felt better since you tsok the first half box 2"

" I have, a lot: better; this afternoon I have done four hours in the hayfield, and that is the first time I have done any work since last December." "That is proof sufficient that you owe your recovery to something ?" " To nothillE.. but Dr. Williams's pink pills,and.l shall be greatly pleased to recommend them highly to anyone, and f hall always Epeak well of them." "Dc you object to this interview being published "I have no objection whatever; you are welcome ta do so."
Acd then the" cured" and the " curious "parted.

another, tool this view, and the colloquy termin- ated without demonstrations of love or regret on either side. That there should have been die. appointment on both sides only proves what requires no proof, that the human race is by nature un- reasonable. • _ _

Some weeks later, paragraphs in the newspapers proclaimed that a marriage had been arranged, and would shortly take place, between Viscount Pennington and Lily, daughter of the late Mr. George Meade. Philip Crossley, whom this intel- ligence reached, through the medium of an evening journal, at his club, started forthwith for Hans- place, where Miss Gisborne lived, in order to enjoy the poor satisfaction of exclaiming: "Didn't I tell you so!" "I don't remember that you did," was the lady's rejoinder, when he had been admitted into her presence and had tired off the above ejaculation; "but, at the same time. I can't see what right yoa have to look indignant." "I'm not indignant," Philip declared; "I don't care a straw. If she be not fair for me, or to me —and I drust say---but really it's of no conse- quence. She may marry anybody she likes without the slightest apprehension of breaking my heart. Come, Bob! you know, if nobody else doe 3, that that is ancient history, and that I have given up •bothering myself about the matter." Miss Bob stroked her chin meditatively, while she contemplated the young man's slightly flushed cheeks. "Well," she resumed, after a pause, "and What is to be the next move? " _

"The next move ?, Oh, the Bankruptcy Court I imagine. I've settled .my racing debts; but my account at the bank is considerably overdrawn, and if other creditors see fit to press for payment.— which I am given to understand is their intention —I shall have to file my petition, that's all. Unfortunately, nobody seems to be pining just at present for a neglected estate and a tumble-down mansion in the Midlands." "If it comes to that," said Miss Gisborn.e, "I'll buy your place ; in many ways, it wc u' d just suit me." "I am sorry for that., my dear old Bob, because ,you can't have it, Not until it has passed out of my possession, anyhow. You needn't mention terms, thank you; I decline them in advance." The worst of it was that he meant what he said, and that Miss Gisborne knew he did.

"Phil,' she exclaimed piteously, "is there no way in which you will allow me to help you ? " There is one way, and only one, in which ra man may permit a woman who is obviously enamoured of him to give him pecuniary assistance. She had no thought of suggesting it; yet—how do su,-.:h unforeseen situations come about ?—at the etpiration of half-an-hour she actually did suggest it. The main thing, after all, was to preserve him from utter ruin; -her personal pride was a small nffair in comparison with the attainment of that 'end; moreover, he was genuinely fond of her, if be was not—as of course he was not—in love with her. _ _

As for Philip, tit May be affirmed that when he took both Miss sob's hands in his and addressed her by sundry affectionate epithets he was less mercenary than an unbiassed spectator would doubt- less have pron-ounced him to be. He made no absurd pretence of addressing her as a lover; ho only said wht, at the moment, was perfectly true— that he cared more for her than for anybody else in the world, and that if he had not cared so much for her, it would have been out of the question for him to a.cmpt all that she was ready to bestow upon him. Perhaps she•understood ; perhaps she did not; in any event, she professed laerself more than satisfirerl. "Only (there must be an end and a finish of betting, said she; "that is my sole stipulation, Thus Eord Pennington's fiancée was speedily made aware that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gtaider, and that the right cf seeking con- solation is open to all. It allay even have occurred to her that her former lovere's consolation was more complete than her own; foe Lord Pennington mas an unaseiable person, whereas evee:Thody liked Mies Bob, and Phil had always been velit, to singher praises. After all, that lucky "Tiling man might well be deemed to have gained more than 'he had lost. He would not now be compelled to part.with the her.ae of his forefathers, and although most of his horses had been brought to the hammer, ihelad decide to retain Missel Thrush, -which was entered for the Leger, and u;kich 'wee still considered by many competent it-ickps to he the best ect-ilt of the year. It never rains but it port. No soccer had. Philip been snatched beck. from the jaws of 'bank- ruptcy to prospective aluene&than his uncle, old David Crossley, stretched out -to .him the right hand of pardon and congratulation. "ou are nest dcor ,to an -imbecile, , rmy boy " _ _ _ _ .

this opulent and childless ironmaster -candidly remarked; "but you are going to marry the most senS:ble woman I have -eye: met, and I believe I can trust her to take -ease the, ,you don't throw good money after bad. So wawai forget the :past." , He made har,te ,to .forgefrthe present, and the Pature into the bargain, by succumbing to a-sudden attack of gout án the-stomach. It was really most considerate of him, and if his nephew, who inherited the eichdle of his large fortune. heaved . . .

; some sighs over what might have-been, these, it is • needless to say, were stifled in the presence of : Miss Bob. It was, indeed, 'manifestly absurd, as ; -will as ungrate63l,•toimlude the winning of Lily IVlez.de amongst ?things whichsmight have been. To begin with, old David had bequeathed his money tovlliss Gisbernes I.uture hushand, as such, 4.nd I .would never hvae,entrusted it to an irresponsible .; k apeadthrift ; added tomhich,R.r. 'girl whose affec- -5 tiers were susceptible of the ~precipitate transfer aisr)layed In Lily could scareelybe accounted worth "Ay iLa i ng. i'hilip, therefore, .not only proclaimed Iristself happy, ii3ut aimost believed in the truth of him assertion.

'it has to be cenfssged that Miss Bob also,lor all ' the good sense with which she was universally atii justly credtiteci, was supreprely happy during I these summer menths. One lusty he very sensible and, , clear-sighted; one may perceiveqw plainly as possi- ble that A cannot be 8.:hr..0r .two plus two produce ars result save feur ; yet belief isi miracles, as all , the world knows, is not-incompatible with.wiedom, - add this homelyavoman, ,who wawunder no 'illusion as -to her homeliness, had !• for years adored the . mat who indignantly scented' her offer to set him ' free, now that he no lenger stood in need of • financial aid. Et had been -arranged that the xcarriage should -take place •in7Tovember, which month (by a mere-coincidence, no doubt) wee:like- vise to witness the nuptials Of :Lord Pennircton snenliss Meade. One can only attribute to mere oincidence the somewhat embarreising ...circumstance that ' both coups were brought together .nc.der the same hoseable north-country-rod early in September. No .nostess, it may fairly .be assumed, would have thus made up her party for the •boncaster meek except through inadvertence, and such wtu; the view taken by the persons concerned, who met without any stupid, -ill-bred,show of discomfiture. Nevertlyless, it was, to -.my the least of it, unfortunate that Philip Crossley and Lily Meade chanced to find themselves the sole ocaupants of the library after the conclusion of • the first day.'..s racing. It would Lase been easy, to he sure, fer t one .of them to get up and leave the room; bat 4 perhaps it would have been ;rather .untlignified to seek ..atiety after that fashior. At all events, neither el them did so. and a„cenversation fraught with peril was the not tinnaturol consequence. "It- cannot make any (difference now," the girl mound up a series of deplorably indiscreet mutual (confessionc by observing. "Oh, •no ; it can't maim any difference now," Whilip sorrowfully agreed. "Only,l,in glad you 'mow the truth, and I am glzid I know the truth; though it comes too late. Ten can't blame me for having 'thought that you 'wished to be rid of an encumbranee—you talked as if you did, that day at Ascot, diau't you ?—and I suppose I ought not to blame you for—for—" Well, it may be that he had no right to blame her for her inability to restrain her 'tears; but of course she had every right to blame him for sucldeon..l3 seizing her in his rims and kissing her wet . -.Aks. He had to beg her pardon wry humbly and promise that he would never again .ns forget himself.

"'But it's hard !—it's horribly bard!" he pleaded. "If I were to be the only one to suffer, I shouldn't mind so much; only when I think of that old brute Pennington —" "You need not suffer from the thought of that old brute Pennington any more," interrupted Miss Meade quietly; "I am not going to marry him." "Lily! do you mean that you will throw him over? '

"I mean that I have thrown him over. I told him this afternoon that the engagement was at an end; so, you see, our explanation has had nothing to do with it. I fancied that I could marry him, but, as the time came nearer, I found I couldn't— that was all."
But was that all? Could that be all? Did not what had passed render another rupture both obligatory and unspeakably desirable? It was a case of conscience, tckbe solved as best he might by

"I take it," observed Lord Pennington tranquilly, while he replaced his field-glasses in their case, after watching the finish for the llardwicke Stakes at Ascot, "that this about puts the extinguishez upon our young friend." "You speak as if you were glad," returned his neighbour, a short., plain-featured lady, whose ago might have been anything between thirty and forty, and whose dark hair displayed threads of grey which she had not thought it worth while to pluck 9ut or dissimulate. "My dear Miss Bob, I ain't glad; I'm awfully sorry. I backed his slug of a colt for a fiver, against my better judgment, at odds on, and— there you are, you see! One said to oneself that, after all, such a moderate horse as Exactitude couldn't give two stone to Missel Thrush; but the fact seems to be that any horsecan give anything to one of Crossley's. Never knew a man so irrevocably doomed to run second or third, nor so confoundedly cocksure of winning! Well, from what I hear of his expenditure this week, he won't own whiners or losers much longer. That's some comfort for those who have been idiots enough to listen to his tips." "A philosophic mind like yours can always dis- covcc compensating features in the calamities of others," remarked Miss Roberta Gisborae as she turned away. _ _

Miss Gisborne was well aware that Lord P.enningtcm, much as he disliked parting with :money, would not really grudge the ten or fifteen ;pounds which his misplaced confidence in poor Philip Crossley might have cost him. She was well aware that that opulent, middle-aged nobleman did xiot love Philip, whereas he did love,--or, at all events, very seriously admired—the beautiful Miss Meade, whose betrothal to Philip was upon the point of being made public. She was well aware, too, that Phi(ip, whose racing career had been brief and disastrous, had plunged recklessly of late; and these things made her pensive. "Miss Bob," as she was called by her intimates, was probably the best friend that that foolish young fellow, Philip Crossley, had in the world. But what is the use of being a man's best friend if he will not let you help Him? Herself 'the only daughter of a once well-Inown magnate el' the turf, who had left her a considerable fortlrne, • Miss Bob was as capable as anybody of giving sound advice respecting racing matters .;'only, as she did not bet, and was convinced, rightV or wrongly, that those who do are bound to corns to grief sooner or later, her advice was not likely to 'move of much avail with a youth who had,once been so unfortunate as to all off a ten-to-one chance in thousands. A rich man, if he bk) an old and tried friend, may, without dioffence, offer a loan to an em- barraosed one—will, tin all probability, indeed, be requested to do so; but a woman friend is otherwise situated. Philip, it might be talsa as certain, would tt?ever accept money from a woman. Moreover, there was a reason of which Miss Gisborne was conscious—sometimes she half- feared that Philip also was conscious of it--t4k,ich rendered her of all,women the least fitted to lay him under an obligation of that nature. She met him presently in the paddock---wtall, handsome; grey-eye fellow, With brown irair-Ohich curled tightly all over his head, in pits of assiduous shearing; and in answer to her anxious question he said, laughing and slarugging his shoulders:
"Oh dear, yesl-Etone broke this journey'l a had to be a case of sink or swim, and—it is now,-3. case of sunk."
"Didn't you buck the colt both waysT" Miss Gishorne asked.

441 did, for a trifle ; but what's the good•of that? 'You were quite ,right, my dear Bob; you always\ are quite right; .and Missel Thrush is an arrant thief. He could 'have won in a common .canter if he had chosen. Well, well, let us hope that he will serve Perinirigton, who wants to buy him, better than he'has served me."

There was no denying that Philip Crossluy was a good loser. Miss Bob could not help :a-dmiring him—but then she never could help admiring him, in spite of all hie provoking follies—as lie walked lightly away. He must have walked straight away from the course, for he was nowhere to be seen when the next event took place. "He has gone to tell that girl," thought Miss B9b, remembering that Lily Meade, .who was -stpying in the same house With him, :had not .accompanied her party to the course that day. "Now the question is: What will she say to him?"

Perhaps that was the question, although Philip -Crossley,' striding swiftly across the heather :towards a belt cif trees which concealed the house at which Miss Meade and he were guests for the race week, did not Think so. He was bound, in his opinion, -to release the girl—bound even to insist upon her accepting release, should she demur. He was completely, irretrievably ruined. His 'horses, his home, everything must be sold without delay; he could not ask or permit any girl to share his coming indigence. Least of all ,could he demand such a sacrifice from an acknowledged beauty, who had no money of her own and who had been notoriously admired by more than one wealthy and titled bachelor. Oh, no; his course ...was obvious, and the sooner he got Through a .Painful quarter of an hour the better it+would be 'for -both parties concerned. If the frailty of his ;mortal nature left him with something of an arriere penste he was mot, to do him justice, aware of entertaining any:

His quick walk—quicker because he did,net want to think more than, he could help—ended on a !broad, smooth lawn, where a tall young woman, ,dressed all in White, was seated under the Shade of .a cedar tree. -She.jumped up at the first sight of .him and advanced, throwing away the illustrated newspaper which she probably had .not been :perusing. "You have lost'!" she cried, in a one ,raLher -affirmative than interrogative. The young man nodded. "Missel Thrush, turned it.t?.p. There was always the danger tiaat.he:might —and he . "

"Ahl that was why I pretended to have a 'headache. I couldn't have gone and looked knowing, as I did, what defeat Must imply." There ,was a momentary silence, during ,whif,h these forlorn lovers .surveyed one another anxiouly and curiously. Then Philip said, with. sigh: "Yes, of course you knew. I didn't ttell•you mEr reason for wishing that our engagement Should he .kept quiet ,until after Ascot; but you guessed ,that the Hardwicke Stakes must make me or iyalk me.'" • "That the loss of th:3 Ilardwicke Stakes must make you break off the engagement, .do you mean ? " asked the girl. She Might, just for form's sake, ',aye looked little more agitated, Philip Cr, ES y thought, i while she, ac it happened, was mai in; a precisely 1 similar inward criticism on his own demeanour. Ile said to himself that, notwithstanding the golden hair, the bright blue eyes and the 'flawless complexion Which he adored, the girl of his 'heart was a heartless girl. She, on the other hand, admitted that her betrothed was handsor.ne, unselfish and brave in his method of facing adversity; hut that he carol much, or ever !had really cared mu, for her she found it imposSible to believe., Had she cherisheds.ny lingering donbt2 as to that, his reply would have 'dispelled them. "Oh, yes," he eaid briskly; "that's one of the inevitable results a having not Zing left to marry upon. Fortunately, nobody has been told that me were engaged." . "Only everybody has inspecte.' "Which isn't quite the same thing, is it?" "Not quite, I suppose." • . . _ . _ . . ,

' Another brief interval of silenee ensued, which Miss Meade broke by asking hesitatingly: "Is what yon said just now really true? Will you have nothing left?" "Practically nothing. Estates can't be disposed of from one moment to another, and one doesn't know for certain what they will fetch; 'but I take it that, at best, I.shall have to make a fresh start with four or five hundred a year. My rich old uncle, as I told you, has formally washed his hands of me, so I need not expect. a shilling from him; and it stands to reason that you and I, having been brought up as we have been, must not dream of a joint fight against penury. I have been a ghastly fool—l won't attempt to make excuses for myself; but, at least, I have just sense enough to be able to distinguish between what is possible and what isn't."

What was, perhaps, impossible was that any self- respecting girl, after such a speech as that, could hold an apparently reluctant swain to his bargain. Lily Meade. who was not lees self-respecting than

div.p: DEATH OF COUNCILLOR LEE.

It is with regret that we annourco the death which took place at hi.; residence, 7, Gra ppenhall-road ,Stonleon kleathion Sunday morning, of Councillor John Lee. The deeeasei gent:ernan, who was in his fifty-seventh years had been ailing for about a month, and a fortnight ago, Dr. Braide was called in and discovered that be waD staffering from congestion of the liver and kidneys. fle was, however, not confined to the hou3e until last Thursday, and death resulted from syncope. The late Councillor was a native of Leigh, but had live& the greater portion of his life in Warrington. During the last ten years he bad carried on the business of a maltster at, e!emises in Winwick-street trading as Messrs Dakin and %ea.?. He was elected to the Town Council in 1894, and was a representative of the Latchford Ward up to the time of his death. Be was vice-chairman of the Water Committee, and a member of several other committees- At the time of the promotion of the Cor- noration Bill, Alderman Franc,mh, chairman of the Water Committee being ill, duties of the • chairmanship devolve d upon the late counciilor,, and at the ratepayers' nuetings at the Gym- nasium and Parr Hall he explained the provisions ef the waterworka scheme. His duties about that time. were extremely onercua, and were efficiently discharged: A strong Conservative, he was a member of the Conser- vative Association, and a vic.-president of the Junior Conservative Association. As a :nark of respect to the deceased gentleman, flags at the Town Hall and Con— servative Club were hoisted at half-mast on Sunday..

div.head: AT CUE RDEN HALL.
div.p: AT CUE RDEN HALL.
Members of the Draughts Clubs' Association have an Enjoyable Outing.

''The deep•rooted intere,t which is c7inced in the Warrington Draughts Clubs' Association by the popular President. Mr R A Naylor, was practically demonstrated on Saturday when the members were invited to spend the afternoon and evening at Mr Naylor's beautiful residence at Thetwat,. A large number availed them- selves of the opportunity, and ace nnpanied by their wives and lady friends. left Cairc-street shortly after two o'clock in brakes, supplied by Mr Edward Coneor the whole of the cost being generously defrayed by Mr Narlor. Fortunately the weather was mast fav ,urable, and the outing proved a great success. Arrived at Cuerden Hall, the party were met on the steps leading into the evalery by Mr and Miss Naylor, a most corc.ial welcome being extended to all. An inspection of the interior of the hcuse, nearly every part of which was thrown opso to the vistors, was first made, followed by. a ramble through the charming grounds. Several out- door games were played, and before adjourning to the Temperance Hall for tea the party who were grouped en the steps of the balcony outside were photographed by Mr E W 'Clarke of Penketh Then a separate group was taken of the members of the LAgue, prominent amongst wir,m were Mr. Frank Dunne (ch,..irm in of the committee), Mr. Clarka (treasurer), and Mr. D Piinston (secretary). Toe championship cup.which is a v ry pretty one, and was originally nresemted by Mr. W. Chalmers, figures in the photograph. It hag been wan two years in succession by the Cairo-street team, and if they are eqoally success- ful next year it will become their pion, ab,elntrir. There are now two divisions in the league—the junior and the senior divisions—ard the janior trophy has also been won by the Caire-street team.

A capital tea was provided by Mr R A and Miss Naylor. in the Temperance Hall, at six o'clockaarnansst those present, in addition to the host and hosres, being Sir William and Lerly Beiley.. of Sale Hall ; the Rev R Postance and Mrs Pretence. .of Liverpool ; the R. 217 and Mrs Macconwell.of Liverpool's the Rev W H Drummond, Mrs Grim-haw, Sale; Mrs A. inlph Renshaw, Sale ; Dr Dyer. Cheltenham ; Mr W Worthington, and Mr G Davidson, Liverpool ; thelHieses Tures:eau, Wavertree ; and Mr and Mrs Shakeshaft. After tea time was afforded for another ramble through the grounds, and a icsnrinuance of the games, and at half-past sewn all I assembled in the gallery atthe Hall to listen to the pro- ' gramme ef music which had been arranged. Mr.Nayssoa said that fort wn years the Cairo-street Club had been succeesful.and he was very pleased to say that Lady Bailey would ehortly ask Mr. Drummand to accept the gift on behalf of the members of the Cairo-street team. They were very pony they were so soon to lose Mr. Drummoed, who was leaving Warrington fora very important appointment in 'Belfast. If the Cairo-street team won the cup next year someone would have to buy another-one, and in the natural course of events he £159. posed the man who would have to do so would be the President. (Laughter.) -S-leeine that the trade of the country was not in a vervlieuriebine condition,and that I they were all beginning to feel a little poverty stricken I—(renewed lauehter)—he honed that those who repre- sented other clubs would bring together such a team I that the plate would net be appron riated by the Cairo- ereet Club for the third time in sun cession. (Lattehter I and appleuse). I Lady BAILEY then stepped forward, and in enio‘ea terms presented the 'cap, which bears the following inscription :—" Warrington and District 'Draughts Clubie etaamnionship cup, presented by W. Chelmers Esq.. 1893-1899 "—to the Rev. W. H. Drummond., on behalf of the Cairo-street team." SieWteraem BAILEY said it was very gratifying to Ladvl3 alley and himself to be privileged to take:start in that very interesting gathering. He had no idea when they'swere invited to pay a visit to Cuerden Hall that tbeyeceould have sults a delightful visit surrounded as they were by numerous articles of utility and /beauty.as well as to assist in a function that was A very agreeable one to him, because as-an Alderman of 25 years' exper- ience of municipal work he had advccated that draughts chess, and other innocent games should be used and -permitted in the free libraries of their municipalities. (Applauee.) The last peper ha read before thelLibrnry Association when it met in Manchester advocated a mursiCipal clubroom being established in evereSward and maintained out of the rates for the benefit of the rate- payers. There was no charity in such an arrangement whatever and ha contended that instead of the libraries and reading rooms being made such monotonous places, and people admonished when they went into them to keep their mouths shut, men ought to be permitted to play at draughts and chrse, to take their wives with them and to have light refreshments such as tea and coffee-a(applause)—and that social improvement should ' no longer depend upon-private enterprise, but should be provided in every ward in every large town •out of the rates 'for the benefit of the ratepayers. In the same way I that they had public parks at the cost of the public, art galleries, swimming baths and many other municipal enterprises, they should also have ward club rooms to be used as a,modification of the Free Libraries Act. Those present would, therefore, see that be was in entire sympathy with the draughts club enterprise. The measure of a man was not bow be spent his time lie the workefnr office, but the manree in which he spent la's leisureehoers. Some toe& to different amusements, and if anyone could invent a method to enable hard-working people to spend their time in a rational manner he woUld.l be doing something to promote civilization 'and public'l happiness. (Applause). This was a favourite topic of I I his, and when he once commenced to speak about it he had considerable difficulty in knowing when to stop. I (Latrehter). He thanked them most cordially for the etreat distinction which had been conferred upon 'Lady Bailey and himself by being asked to assist in the ceremony, and h'e hoped he would be invited to attend on another occasion. (Hear, hear and applause). Three cheers having been given for Sir 'William and 'Lady 'Bailey. • The'Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND delivered a short address, in the (mum of which he said be had much pleasure, on behalf of the members of the Cairo-street teams, in accepting the cup and-the draughts boards which were. the visible emblems of the success which had been earned during the past season. He felt -particular gratification that the hard work of the Secretary of the League had been largely instrumental in the success of thattiseague. It was also gratifying that his own team had wonthe cup two years in succession. And now it only remained for him to veice the unanimous feeling of the members of all the teams present, and /11-81 of the wiver and sweethearts, when he thanked Mr. and Miss Naylorler their kind hoepitelity wh:ch .had iven exu tendedte them on that occasion. The members of the Leaenehoped that Mr. Nafinr would remain their presi- dentior some time to come, and that it might possibly enter into his mind and his kindly heart to again eels the members to visit his ' house, and in that way enable themtrehecome even bettersequaitsted than they were already. Be asked them to extend to Mr. and Miss Nsylor their most hearty thartlas for the kind hospitality which had been extended tothem that day. (Applause.) The request was heartily eotnplird with, three cheers being given for the host•and hostess. The concert was then proceeded with, the first item being a duet by Mr and Miss Naylor, which was well sung and warmly applauded. 'Dr Drer,who is on aarisit to Cuerden 'Hall, rendered a pianoforte sale, and FO pleased the audience that nothing less than a repetition or another solo would satisfy them. Another pitce, equally attractive and equally 'well played was caetri- buted. The glee singers were heard to advantage in " Minstrels Three," hut their best effert was " Retain I Adair," which wan sung very sweetly. Mr H Ashcroft followed with a song entitled "John Bull's letrer bag," and Mrs Eden earned hearty plaudits for a tasteful T,„._ 1 dering of "Sweet Genevieve." Mr Nestor, at the re- quest of his visitors, favoured with a patriotic song,ard. intreeponse to an encore he gave en excellent reoiratipn of his own composing, entitled " The Three Sisters:" A very successful concert was brought to a cow:linden with the singing of " el save the'Queen." Having said " good-here '" to the kind hoet and hostess the parry lett the hall for the 'Mars in waiting ontside, and when Wartingtnn wee safely reached it was vneed that the outing had been the most successful in the history of the Association.

div.head: Volunteer Intelligence
div.p: Volunteer Intelligence

On Saturday afternoon the Volunteers had a march out to Stockton Heath. returning by Latch- ford. The battalion paraded at the Drill Hall at four o'clock, under the command of Major Buckton. The muster numbered 450. The cyclist company, under the command of Lieutenant Gough. went on reconnaissance duty between Stocktrn Heath and High Legb. The remainder of the battalion, owing to shortness of time, did not carry out, any tactical scheme. Prior to their departure from Vie Drill Hall, Major Buckton presented Sergeant Ha mpson with a long-service medal.
