Parsee, to say nothing of Jews, Roman Catholics, and many descriptions of Nonconformists. Control by Parliament is therefore objected to and resisted. There is even less inclination to accept the rulirig of the Archbishops and the Bishops They cannot, it is contended, make the law, but only administer it. We are rapidly drifting into an impasse. The second method of curing the bickerings, unrest and divisions of the Church is its separation from the State, its complete self- government. But many thinkers hesitate at this point, and fling out their phrases in rebuke of the Disestablishmentarians. Yet there is no surer and no better remedy for the ills of the time. Let the Church be organised on its own basis, making its own creed, its own courts, its own dis- cipline. In no other way can chaos be turned into cosmos. Advocates of this plan are not irreli- gious. It is admitted that religion is as strong in the colonies and in the -United States, where there is no established religion, as it is in this country where unbiassed foreign • observers, coming to ris with eyes and minds undisturbed by preposses- sions, describe church-going as a part of good breeding and current fashion, and nothing more. There is, of course, the question of the endow- ments, and it is a huge difficulty. Plundering God is a smart phrase often applied to the pro- ject, but it hurts no sincere mind. The State ha given and the State can take away. Everything must be judged by what is best for ecclesiastical peace and religious progress. The devout will always subscribe for their own faith, and it looks like plundering when once Catholic endowments are diverted to Protestant purposes, and vice ver6a. The country must see before long that this strife it! the Church is injurious to religion, and that the only way to heal it and to give the various forms of laith fair play is to sever the connection between Church and State. It has ceased to serve any use- ful purpose, and useful communities never think of setting up the connection as either a wise or practicable thing.
Politics are nothing if A Look Ahead. they are not speculative.

The idea of a closer union between such Liberal Unionists as still remain Liberals and the Liberals who have not bowed the knee to the god JINGO is very timely and agree- able, and we hope it may come abou t. It would be an excellent thing to reduce the number of divisions in the Liberal party, and to restore its strength by unity upon such topics as are of pres- sing interest. But we must not suffer ourselves to be the victims of any illusions, and it is distinctly illusory to think that the Irish question, now so passive, will long remain in its present condition. Mr. REDMOND expressed his belief on Saturday that "Home Rule was nearer than most people imagined." The famous O'CONNELL was constantly saying the same thing about REPEAL, and he died without its accomplishment having been obtained. Still, we must look a little ahead, and INF . not suffer ourselves to be deceived by the idea that Home Rule is far away, or obscured, or hardly likely to resume its importance as a burn- ing question in our time. Any circumstances which altered to a large extent the present strength and relations of parties might bring it to the front again. It might come as a part of the new Imperialism, which is based upon local independence and central unity. The Federa- tion of Australia may help it forward, not only as an ideal but as a practical policy. The Australians may remind us of some points we are in danger of forgetting. The Irish regiments, which have done so well for us in South Africa,may teach us a lesson we had :suffered to be obscured, and which was seldom absent from Mr. GLADSTONE'S mind—the lesson that our Empire has been largely built up by the deeds of men who we had been warned were eager to destroy the Empire. Nor can we over- look the fact that a General Election may not be far off, and that it may change a good, deal, and is expected to do so. The result of that election is always, and most unwisely, regarded as a foregone conclusion. It may be a surprise for us in one of two ways. It may give the Unionists a smaller majority, it is conceivable, though apparently improbable, that it might give the Liberals a small majority. Were either result to come, the Irish question would cease to be where it is now. If the Unionists had no strong majority, the temptation to settle the Irish question would be very great. If Liberals and Unionists were pretty nearly equal, the Irish members would hold the balance of power, and then events @would take a most dramatic turn. If the Unionists did not cede some form of Irish self-government, the Liberals would propose to do so. Take the com- mon expectation—that the Unionist majority were increased. How would that affect the Irish ques- tion ? According to the Unionist belief it would kill it absolutely. We are not sure that it would do anything of the kind. A resolute Irish minority could do a great deal. Governing Ireland would not be so very easy if the Irish leaders were minded to revive the days of the Irish League, and M.P.'s were ready to go to prison. Federation of the Empire might be further developod,and in that way the colonies could do a great deal to further the Irish claim already admitted to be just by nine out of every ten colonials. Hence we cannot shut our eyes to the Irish question, in our eagerness to reunite with some of our old friends. We had rather they were able to see that the maintenance of the Union is not worth an outbreak of militar- ism, of extravagant exp enditure, and of general political reaction. These impressions will come in time. It is in this direction that the most hope- ful unity will come. But who can say what is immediately ahead in domestic politics?

THE proposal to construct a light railway or tramway between Windermere and Ambleside has aroused a/strong protest from those who are opposed to the further desecration of our English Alps. The "groan from ttie Lake District " against the scheme is:making itself heard very per- ceptibly in London. But the protestors against the threatened vandalism come from all parts o,c. the country. There is little doubt that "trams, whether steam or electric, will tend to destroy the charms of a choice bit of scenery. Ikideed the proposed tramway is enough to make the philose- pher of Brantwood turn in his grave. It cannot be said that the Lake Country is not sufficiently' accessible already. It is surrounded by railvvaYs and the peacefulness of its more charming valleys is now broken by the shriek of the railway whistle. There was some excuse for the construction of the small narrow-gaug° railway up the lovely Eskdale valley to the foot ot Scawfell, for it was originally mineral line, and there were iron mines whose ore wanted carrying. It would destroy the beau** of the district less to have this carried by a Will! narrow-gauge line than to cart it by road. BD" the proposal made someyears ago to construct similar line up the wilder Ennerdale was defeated. There is no " mineral wealth " excuse for a tram- way from Bowness to Ambleside, past classic spots endeared to us by literary association as w°ll as. romantic beauty. It is only intended ftohr "trippers," who might surely be content ri t 'bus, char-it-bane and waggonette. Doubtlesswthse local population favour it, for it would bring g to their mill. But the Lake District is the Oar' ground of the nation—one of the playgrOlindS, indeed, of the civilised world ; and there is 0105 fore sound reason why what remains of its nata'a beauty, already somewhat marred by man, 3b09 'be preserved from further disfigurement DY uglier utilities of civilisation.

----- According to a correspondent of the " who gives a review of recent decisions on the P°'" ; the question whether a bicycle is a vehicle ° carriage may now be taken to be finally settled:— in favour of the bicycle, but against the rider. Ti'e cycle is not a "glorified foot," like a roller skat,e: or a stilt, or a crutch, or even a walking-stick. it carries its rider it is a carriage. The cyclist Ilass been for a quarter of a century in an anoinalollt position in the eyes of the law—analogous to ths, of the creature which could neither be describea as flesh, fisb, fowl, nor good red-herring. But a number of local Acts bicycles have been include(' among the carriages, and reading general Acts rfr ferring to conveyances in the light of these, the judges in a recent appeal case defined the' position, thus very precisely if prosily: "AijB mechanical contrivance which carries peoP,:: or weights over the ground, carrying tw" weights, or lifting the people oft their own feet,n that the foot of man and the body or trunk 0,; man do not support his own weight, is a carriagt and it does not matter " that the man who '7, carried gives his own propulsion to the carriage... Ergo: A bicycle is a carriage. But even that do 6! not settle the question. When a bicycle does 1201' carry the man, but is wheeled quietly by him 9, u his side, is he entitled so to wheel it along a public footpath, like a perambulator? Or is it legallyeo; eluded therefrom because it is a carriage ? Th" point appears yet to be in doubt; there has bee° no definite judicial opinion given upon it. Thel will, we are afraid, have yet to be a special Act Parliament devoted to the cyclist. The cycle, well as the cyclist when he rides it, is still vet/ much in the position of Mohammed's coffin, atle- pended between earth and Heaven.

The latter seers much at home in dealing severe blows with his Pv`-, as with his 4.7 guns. WITH a General Election Chaos in the near at hand the Church of Church.

England is in full crisis. The rival bodies are demonstrating. The Church Association is organising electors and looking after candidates on the purely Protestant basis. The English Church Union desir.es to get rid of Erastianism and to establish ecclesiastical tribunals and restore the Catholic ideal and practice. The Church Reform League desires to establish self- government for the Church without destroying the connection between Church and State. These bodies are all active, and endeavouring to attract attention by a parade of numbers, precedents, and ideals. The result is rather embarrassing. The Protestants assure us that they are the majority, if not of clergy, at least of laymen. When State connection is advocated by Protestants the apathetic or sceptical assure us that the Romanisers are a feeble folk and need hardly be taken into account. On the other hand, the Romanisers de- dare that they are far too numerous to be prose- cuted or ignored. What, under these circum- stances, is a plain Churchman or any ordinary politician to think and do? He is bewildered,and if he be a logical man he is bound to con- template a state of affairs in which these feuds will cease. Only two ways of achieving peace present themselves to his mind.. The first is that Parliament shall set up a standard and enforce it by law, putting down Romanising extravagances and maintaining the undoubted Protestatism of the National Church. This course of action is less easy every year. Parliament is full of work in adjusting an old and unwritten Constitution to the needs of the time, and Parliament is no longer composed of members of the Church of England. Ever since 18:29 Parliament has been changing into a representation of all creeds. It even contains a

THAT HOPE DEFERRED MAKETH THE HRART SICK is just as true now as ever it was will be attested by all whose most cherished aspirations Wive remained unfulfilled. In every walk of life we encounter this hankering after the (supposed) unattainable, whilst in many cases the remedy is close at hand if those interested only knew how to even themselves of it. It affects most businesses, the furnishing trade especially. For instanee, a young man meets a maiden fair whose appearance and merits he approves. She, likewise, appreciates his qualities, and quickly an affection springs up between them. How pleasant they think it would be to marry and start housekeeping together. Then the stumbling block presents Itself--where is the cash to purchase furniture to come from ? With him, time past, like with most young fellows, "enough for the day has been the evil thereof." rington and other towns below the city's outfall have suffered long enough from the sewage sent down upon them. The Ship Canal has been the vehicle utilised and we may hope for purer waters in the future now that Manchester is pledged to remedial action.

We have been looking in vain for the commence- ment of court and alley open-air concerts in War- zington. This is a movement which has been taken up earnestly and energetically in a number of towns and cities, and it gives promise of great development. In Liverpool it has been the ,means of adding a little brightness to many a dark alloy. -Bands of voluntary soloists and instrumentalists have supplied concerts in the open-air in back alleys and courts to appreciative audiences com- posed of the very poor. It is much akin to the movement originated in Warrington by Mr George Thompson, for providing concerts inside the Work- house, and which has been so successful. There should be little difficulty in extending the good work to some of the slams of the town. It is perhaps getting too late to make a commence- ment this year, but it is certainly a work which should be attempted in Warrington.

The majority of people in Warrington will have only a very hazy notim of the amount of business done at the various cattle markets in the town. They have little opportunity of learning much on this bubject, as their only means of estimating the number of animals changing hands is by calculat- ing the number of semi-wild cattle they have to dodge in the public streets during a given period; and this is a laborious and uncertain method. But we see from reports on the condition of the sale yards presented to the Board of Agriculture by their Inspectors, and forwarded to the Markets Committee of the Corporation,that during a period of six months there were exposed for sale at the "Norton Am s" and "Eagle and Child" yards the large number of 1,387 cattle, 798 calves, and 1,126 sheep. These are striking figures and, in addition to the unsatisfactory state of the yards, present a very strong argument in favour of the early provision of a public cattle-marEet and abattoir. There is evidently a very big business done in Warrington in this line, and the consider- ations of public health and safety, and the con- venience of the farmers themselves, demand some such common market. The question has been be- fore the Council on many previous occasions but of late seems to have been lost sight of in the con- bideration of more ambitious schemes in other directions. We trust it will come to the fore again and attain early realisation.

The decadence of the French nation is to be seen in the laws that the alarmed legislature are now passing. It is not generally known that the decrease in population has brought about the imposition of severe penalties on any person who gives an infant under one year any form of solid food unless medically ordered; and nurses are for- bidden at any time or under any pretext to use nursing bottles with rubber tubes. Other equally strange and stringent laws have been recently enacted by the French Government, which, des- pairing of obtaining any increase in the birth-rate, lis devoting its attention to keeping alive the few children that are born.

It seems almost a pity that the inhabitants of Mafeking were not reduced to even more desperate straits than obtained during the recent siege, for their privations and difficulties only served to de- velop the adaptability and resourcefulness of Gan. Baden-Powell and others. Wears told that a Scotch- man invented a new kind of porridge which satisfied the hunger of the poorer people when the supply of other eatables gave out. The scarcity of cash or, currency of any descrip- tion, induced General Baden-Powell to set his Wits working in another direction that than of circumventing his foes, and with the assistance of Mr. E J Ross, an amateur photographer, photo- graphic £1 notes were turned out at the rate of 20 per day. The General sketched the design for the note and drew an ingenious picture indicating the" defence and defiance" of the town, for the purpose. In another column will be fonnd an Interview with the clever photographer whose ssistance was so valuable to the General in found- leg the" Mafeking Mint" in a "dug-out." The article is very readable and indicates the readiness and cheerfulness with which Baden-Powell and his merry men were prepared to meet all emergencies. Ft is quoted from "Photography," which has some excellent illustrations for the interview including a reproanction of the £1 note itself..

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

Lord Roberts's announcement of the annexation of the Transvaal not only brings the war formally to a close' without really ending the ckmpaign. but it has had the eDct of giving a very decide-I fillip to preparations in the provinces for the approach- ing General Election. The dissolution of Parlia- ment may come any day; the capture of Mr. Kruger, plain " Mister" now, and an arrangement of the terms of peace being all that is needed to give the finishing touch to the picture. Unionists are not at all unmindful of the advantage of appeal- ing to the country while a spirit of patriotism animates the people, and before the letters of Dr. Clarke and Messrs. Labouchere and Ellis tire for- gotten. At an ordinary time the reasons given for hurrying matters might justify such action; but,as the British public have tte right to pronounce an opinion, as to what shall be the future administra- tion of the two new colonies, it is hoped and ex- pected that the present Government, before asking for the support of the electors,will issue a clear and definite statement of the broad principles upon which government is to be established in the Trans- vaal and the Orange River Colony. It is,moreover, important that without any needless delay the enemies of this country and foreign Powera should understand that England has a fixed policy, which will not be changed by a General Election.

Publicans who allow card playing in bar-parlours for drinks or for money, are cautioned by the Bir- mingham licensing magistrates refusal to renew the licences of certain public-houses and beerhouses which were objected to by the police on the ground that the occupants had allowcd gambling of that kind, and in bagatelle playing, or of serving police men on duty and other objectionable practices,

This must be a very profitable time for jam manu- facturers, and one would imagine that the good house-wife might do worse than give the matter a thought. Apples and plums are so plentiful in East Ksnt that it does not pay to picipthem. Many growers are allowing the people to have the fruit for picking and taking it away, and it is said that instances have occurred ot farmers, after paying the carriage to LDndon, receiving only sixpence per bushel, involving considerable loss. Yet there are people who to this day affect to treat lightly Mr. Gladstone's well remembered advice on jam- making and small garden culture.

Sound and practical advice was tendered by Sir James Woodhouse, M.P., to the members of the rades Congress assembled at Huddersfield this week. No good, he said, could arise from impatient denunciation of those who did not at once agree with their opinions. If this advice is taken to heart and followed out, not only in the spirit but in the deed, there will be a great deal less un- pleasantness between employer and employed in the future than there is now.

As a factor in the suppression of the plague at Glasgow, the rat catcher appears likely to rank with the medical specialist. It has now been aseer- tai ed that the outbreak is similar to one in Austra- lia/and a Colonial expert who has tlais week visited the stricken city, expressed an opinion that the disease was being spread by rats. The Glasgow health authorities have consequently set experi- enced men to extirpate the rats in the infected area. The Glasgow City Council may well be imagined praying for the advent of the Pied Piper of Hamelin,

Happily the calamity which threatened the trade of South Wales, and many industrial interests, was averted by the Taff Vale men agreeing to refer the case of the signalman, which had caused so much of a tempest in a teacup, to the arbitrament of the Board of Trade, and to drop the principle, or point of etiquette, as the reader chooses, of being repre- sented by their trades' union officials. The difficulty of representation was got rid of owing to the action of the two principal representatives of the men's society having consented to retire to the back- ground in the cause of peace, which was certainly very creditable on their part. They recognised that under Sir W. T. Lewis's scheme the representation of the men will be permanently provided for in the future. So that there has been no sacrifice of principle, The Railway Company have been in- duced by Sir Thomas Lewis to reinstate the men within one month instead of two, whose places had been filled by imported labour during the stiike. While this is all satisfactory enough, so far as it goes it is impossible to ignore the circumstance that the general situation in the railway world is full of ominous clouds. Whether they will pass harm- lessly away, or gather and burst, has yet to be seen. Much will depend, it is believed, on the result of the Great Eastern • and one or two other disputes to which the public attention has been drawn. It is generally conceded that the rate of wages of rail- way men has not advanced in the same rates as that of other trades ; that is to say, the men have not shared to the same extent as the working-classes generally, in the increased prosperity which the country has enjoyed of late years. But as between the men and their employers, there is much to be said on both sides, when the time for saying it arrives.

" Engineering " states that the cost of the main- tenance of ways and works on the twenty principal English, Welsh, and Irish railways in the first half of this year was £3,741,451. The cost in the corres- ponding period of the preceding year was £3,675,727. Thus it will be seen that the general result was an increase of £65,724 The outlay in these departments of railway working has accord- ingly remained practically stationary, as there has, of course, been some increase during the past twelve months in the length of line maintained.

The schedule of charges for wAter for other than domestic purposes published by the Truro Water Company imposes five shillings per quarter for "photography." This it has been understood by certain residents was the charge upon the profes- sional photographer only,regardless of photographic tyros. But even the amateur now finds himself taxed to the same tune, which is causing no little discord in the Cornish City, and in Cornish news- papers. The novice does not rawer to be unreason- able, inasmuch as he is quite willing to pay some- thing extra to pose as a "photographer," but thinks he should not be on the same plane exactly as the professional for simply "exercising" his" hobby." This item is not produced in the interests of water companies, municipal or private, and it is trusted that it may not be regarded in the light of a "wrinkle." For the amateur really is deserving of sympathy,and of ennuragement rather than double taxation. One would be glad to hear if water com- panies generally looked at the matter in this latter light.

John Bull would have a sorry time of it if he were to take seriously half the reports that reach him from across the Channel. Here is one, for instance, of a new gun of the Crausot type, which' should eclipse all guns of any make or patt..rn, hitherto produced by medal man anywhere. The monster piece of artillery is to have an effective range of twenty miles, and will be tried at the fort at Calais sometime soon. Now the straits of Dover at the nearest points between France and England are sixteen miles; 80 that a gun of this description would be able to drop shells on this side of the water, "very comfortably," as a writer on the sub- ject says. There is a big "but," however, even here, let it be added for the greater " comfort "of those whom it may concern, since the idea is not exactly new, and all attempts hitherto made to give it effect have failed, after a few times, to answer the expectations which a few enthusiasts had enter- tained.

The ideal Post-office sketched by Mr. Henniker- Heaton in the " Times " has provoked a great deal of correspondence, and may possibly lead to greater attention being paid to postal affairs in the future. There is manifestly a consensus of opinion against the Post Office being made a revenue department. As most political thinkers are aware, there has long been too much attention paid to revenue and too little to public convenience. There is an evident lack of elasticity, and the officials, from the Secre- tary down, are hide-bound in red tape. Mr. Heaton has fought bravely against this, and deserves the thanks of the pablic for so doing.

Patrick Duggan, an Irish labourer, was on Tues- day morning brought before 'lr. W. Handley, on a charge of drunkenness.—After pleading guilty Duggan said he was not so drunk but that he could walk 50 miles.—The magistrates said there was suffi.lient outside evidence to prove the man was drunk; for it was notorious that he had created a great disturbance in the streets.—Prisoner said he had been seeing his " mite" home.— \lr. There was a lair attendance at the meeting of this brotherhood on Sunday afternoon, when Mr T Harrison occupied the chair, and delivered a concise address on" Earneitness." Miss A Harrison sang with telling effect" I gave my life for thee " and "Cast thy bread upon the water." An excellent address on " Muscular Cnristianity " was given by Mr D Close. l'he speaker quoted incidents which had come under his notice where it had bean essential for a Christian to be a muscular man. The address was greatly appreciated. PREDATORY RUNCORN' BOATHEN.

At Runcorn Police Court on Saturday before Messrs. G. L. Davies and A. R. Norman, Charles Osborne, aged 14 years was charged with stealing a hay fork, the property of sir. Thomas Baxter, C.C., farmer, Dutton Hall. The bay's father, Charles Osborne was charged with receiving the fork know- ing it to be stolen. From the evidence it appeared that the elder Osborne is the master of two narrow boats named the Midas and the Milo belonging to Messrs. Simpson Davies and Co. On the 25th August the boats were passing a field occupied by Mr. Baxter at Dutton, where men were busy harves- ting. A man named Sumner, employed as hand by Osborne, heard the father shout to the son "Are you going for a fork." Thereupon the son went into the field and on his return Sumner heard something dropped into the hold of the boat. Sumner gave information to the police and when the boats arrived at Runcorn, P.C. Wylie went aboard and found the fork. The initials TB. had been cut. from the fork.—The father attempted to make the mas is- tratesbelieve that he did not know the fork was on his boat until the policeman found it. but railed and as he had been twice previously convicted of felony he was sentenced to six weeks hard labour. The son, who denied stealing the fork, was bound over to come up for judgment when called Upoll. DEATH OF A FORMER RUNCORN CITRA.TE IN

div.head: INDIA.
div.p: INDIA.

The" Runcorn Parish Magazine " of the current month contains an account of the death, on the 27th June last, of the Rev. J. D. Ozanne, formerly curate at tbe Runcorn Parish Church. The Vicar thus refers to the deceased gentleman :—Mr. J. D. Ozanne was ordained to the curacy of the parish of Runcorn at the Lent ordination in 1837. He made himself much beloved in his short ministry, when he had for his colleagues Mr Holden, of Antrobus, and the Rev J Bryant, now an incumbent in the diocese of Oxford. He was a man of singular sweetness and gentleness of disposition, a thorough gentleman, and a good scholar. He was educated at Oxford, and loved books as well as human beings. His healtb,never goodegave wavond he was obliged to leave Runcorn in the early summer of 1858. Af'er a short time in Somersetshire, he went out to the Melanesian Mission, living for some years in Norfolk Is!and, where he soon mastered several of the languages of the Archipelago. He found, how- ever. that he was not sailor enough for the con- stant voyages from island to island, in small boats, of which the missionary had to be captain as well as cargo, and returned to Cheshire, b coming in- cumbent of Mossley, near Congleton, for two or three years, until the longing for mission work s.nt him to the Bombay Presidency. He was a man you could not help loving. Some of us affectionately called him the" little curate." Ido not doubt they could write on his tomb the old Christian epitaph, "In pace," nor need I shun to join the spirit of the pathetic pagan prayer" Sit tibi terra levis"—may the earth lie light upon thee. RUNCORN SONS OP TEMPERANCE.

A meeting of the above association was held in the Greenway-road School on Saturday evening. The president (Mr. Thomas R. Whyte) took the chair. Mr. D. Bisbrown gave an address on "Lord Peel's Report on the Licensing Questioa," and stated that the country spent annually £164,000,000 on intoxicating liquors. This was admitted on every hand to be an excessive amount. When the present Government came into power the tem- perance sentiment was so strong in the country that they felt that something must be done. A Royal Commission was appointed, consisting of 24 mem- bers, and evidence was received from all quarters. The Commission sat for over two years, and their report was issued about eighteen months ago. The minority report was more favourable to temperance legislation, and was signed by Lard Peel, Archbishop of Canterbury, Sir Charles Cameron, Ntessrs H H Dickenson, W Allen, W S Caine. Herbert Roberts, and Thomas P Whittaker. Both reports recommended a large reduction in the number of public-houses, and money compensation to those whose houses were closed. Lord Peel's report recommended that there should be one liqour shop to every 750 persons in towns and one to 400 in the country. The owners of those remain- ing would pay an extra annual licenee rent, and thus a fund would be formed to pay off those which were to be closed. The time limit in England and Wales was seven years and in Scotland five years Those who signed the minority report maintained that there was no legal claim, but compensation would be given as a matter of expediency and grace Among many recommendations were the follow- ing :--kppeals to quarter sessions to be abolished; two licensing courts (one for appeals), both have a representative element; earlier closing on week days; reduction of hours of sale on Sunday; aboli- tion of grocers' licences; sale of liquor to children to be prohibited: the tied-house system to be abolished. On the suggestion of a number of mem- bers it was decided to have the discussion on the report at the next meeting.

div.head: SAD SUICIDE OF AN OLD Mir AT WIDNES.
div.p: SAD SUICIDE OF AN OLD Mir AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Saturday morn- ing, Mr S Brighouse investigated the circumstances connected with the death of an old man named William Sanderson,who resided at 79,Cholmondeley- street.—Mr A Bort,hwick was the foreman of the jury.and Sergeants Carter and Williams represented the police.---John Sanderson deposed that the deceased was his father. He was a farm labourer, and was aged 73 years. About two years ago, owing to ill-health, he came from Cambridge to live with witness at Widnes. Since that time he had suffered greatly from diarrhw ',and had been atten- ded by Dr Creighton Hutchinson. About 10 o'clock on August 23rd deceased retired to bed in his usual spirits. The following morning witness got up about 5.30, and upon going into the back kitchen he found the door unlocked. Upon looking around he missed his father's slippers, and went down to the closet ; the door was closed. He pushed it open and saw deceased lying on the floor covered with blood. After carrying deceased into the kitchen be summoned Dr. Hutchinson, who found a wound two inches long on the left side of deceased's throat. The doctor dressed the wound. Witness examined the closet, and found a butcher's knife smeared with blood. His father remained in a semi-conscious condition until Wednesday morning when he died,Dr. Hutch- inson having attended him during that time.--The Coroner: Had you any suggestion that your father would take his life ?—Witness : None whatever, sir.—Neither by his acts or words ?—No sir.—Has he seemed depressed in his mind ?—He has been so since my mother died. He has felt it a great deal. Her death took place about two years ago.— Had he any trouble of any sort ?—No sir.—Sergeant Williams stated that about 10 30 on August 24th, receiving information from Dr. Hutchinson, he went to the last witness's house. Deceased was in ' bed. Witness asked him how the affair happened, but he made no reply. He was quite conscious. He had since seen the deceased twice, but although he was conscious, he would give no reason whatever for his act. The house was beautifully clean, and deceased appeared to have every Droisiblo attention. —The jury returneti a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane.'

div.head: ILICENSING PROSECUTION AT PRODSIIIM
div.p: ILICENSING PROSECUTION AT PRODSIIIM

B3fora Messrs. Charles Reynolds (chairman), A. Thomas and G C Taylor, at the Sessions House, Frodsham, on Wednesday, David Ellams, licensee of the " Traveller's Hest," Five CrossFs,was prosecuted by the police for serving a drunken man on the 30th of July last.—Mr E S Giles, solicitor, Chester, was for the police: and Mr W II Churton, solicitor, Chester, defended.—ln his opening statement Mr Giles said from the information at his disposal it was clear the police had found a drunken man in a field near to the defendant's house, and as it would be admitted the man had received drink at the house of the defendant; from the state the man was in when he left, it might be reasonably supposed that he was drunk when served by the barmaid; and, that being so, he contended that the defendant was responsible for the acts of his agent. A quantity of evidence was heard and after a very short deliberation the Bench dismissed the case.—Alexandra Drinnan,a witness in the case then asked the Bench to allow him two days' ex- penses. He had lost that much through having to attend. The only money he had received was 33 6d for railway fare and that did not cover it.—Super- intendent Nield stated that the witness had given them a written statement upon which they had practically got the case up. 11l fact, only for that statement there would have been no prosecution As the witness had gone in direct contravention to the statement he objected to pay any expenses. Had he substantiated his statement, whatever the result of the case he would have applied to the Chief Con- stable for his expenses in the ordinary way.—The Bench refused to make any order.—Drinnan : Then let me have the Chief C3ustable's address.—Super- intendent Neild : All right I will give yea that. (Laughter.) SAVAGE ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.

MichafriFiTb-u-rnTiFeitiliOr-street, was summoned at Widnes on Monday for b-ing drunk and dis- orderly, and also with assaulting Sergeant Carter and P.C. Mess ilizter whilst in the execution of their duty on Saturday.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.— Sergeant Carter stated that at 11.15 on Saturday night a woman named Mrs. Murphy came to the Police Station and informed him that two of her lodgers were fighting. On going to the place he found the prisoner drunk and using bad language. Witness asked him to be quiet. Mrs. Murphy asked witness to open the door to see where the other man was. As soon as he got into the lobby the prisoner rushed inside and seir,d him by the throat, saying" You are inside now." He struck him on the head and kicked him very violently on the legs and body. After they had been struggling together for fifteen minutes Mrs. Murphy ran to the Police Station and brought P.C. Messen- ger. When they got him to the Police Station he commenced kicking and striking at everything that he came near. On trying to put him into the cell Messenger was kicked on the right leg and badly bruised. Witness was very sore, and scarcely able to walk about.—P.C.'s Messenger and Flitcroft gave corroborative evidence, the last-named remarking that he never saw a rougher prisoner.—Mrs Murphy also gave corroborative evidence —Superintendent , Keighley asked the bench to deal severely with the man, as that class of offence had become too preva- lent.—The Mayor said the assault was entirely uncalled for. Prisocer was mulcted in a fine of 2s 64 and costs for. being drunk, and seven days' imprisonment in each case of assault without the option of a fine.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY' A CORMISPONDENT.]

The Frodsham bench of magistrates last Wednes- day, had before them a rather interesting case, in which Henry Ernest Rowlands, an employee of the "Crown Oooperies," Warrington,was sum,noned for driving a horse and cart without a light. The peculiarity of the case arose from the fact that Row- lands had been served with a similar summons for an offence committed at Daresbary, at which place the summons was dismissed owing to Rowlands Proving that he was not the "defendant." At Frodiham Rowlands urged the same plea very sac- cassfully, and got the case again dismissed. The sequel—if I my call it such—appears to be a pecu- liar one also ; fer Rowlands applied for' expenses. 'Now, under ordinary circumstances, he might have got them too; but Rowlands wag unwise enough to state that he knew who was in cJiaree of the cart" at the time," consequently no expenses were allowed! Superintendent Nield drolly hinted he would summon Rowlands to prove the case azainst the real offdnder and I can't help thinking if he did the process would be an extremely interesting ,I one.

Another case tried before the same court that' excites a little comment, was one in which two men, named Garner and Midge, pleaded guilty to chargzs of" refusing to quit licensed premises ' and drunk and ni.orderly. Of course, the Bench know their duty best. and may hare a glod reason for doing what they did do. But, a layman like my self fails to see why Garner, whn was the least notorious of the tw3. should be fined more than Midge. against whom Superintendent Neill re• marked there were a "page full of rec3rds. and the beginning of the next." Arid, furthermore from the evidence it was apparent t 3 the most casual ob- server, that, if there was any worst of "two had 'tins." that worst was Midge. But then the Frodsham Bench are not to be understood easily. and perhaps these things are only to be exp-cterl from a bench capable of getting behind the " con- cience "of a " comcientious objector."

Runcorn is very much agitated at present owing to the football malady. For the fear of the "lion" is in them. Last year Runcorn twice defeated the Swinton team—at home by 11 points to 3, and at Swinton by eight points to nil. But the outlook for Saturday's meeting is vary glum. An accident to Jimmy Butterworth, who twist:ei his knee at a practide match has proved more serious than at first anticipated, and he is now under Dr Jones, of Liverpool On Saturday last too, S Houghton, was injured in the head and knee and J Faulkner had his knee very badly strained. It is doubtful whether the two latter can take the field, and it is an assured fact that Butterworth will not be able to don the jersey. Thus do matters stand, and hence the fear and trembling at Runcorn.

The Runcorn Urban District Council in a dis- cussion, short but instructive, dwelt upon the desirability of early interments of corpses, AqDBCi- ally in cases of infectious or contagious diseases. Apropos of the same subject. a reference to the objects of the Church Burial, Funeral and Mourning Reform Association, will not be out of place. They are: —(1) The exercise of economy and simnlicity in everything appertaining to the funeral: (2) The disuse of crape. scarves, feathers, velvet trappings and the like. (3) The use of plain hearses or wheeled biers. (4) The avoiding of floral decora- tions. (5) The discouraging. on occasion of the funeral. as far al possible, of ail eating and drinking beyond that of every-day life. (6) The meeting in the church or cemetery instead of at the house of mourning. (7) The disollling of the idea that all the insurance money should be spent on the funeral. (S) The early interment of the body in soil sufficient and suitable for it 3 resolution

t) its canstituent elements. (9) The use of such materials for the coffin tie will rapidly decay after burial. This method is in accordance with the laws of nature, and avoids sanitary evil, while the practice of burying in almost imperishable coffins is fraught with danger to the public health.

If those objects were adopted by the public gen- eral:y, much would be accomplished, and the danger referred to, and the possibilities of epidemic would be more remote. I would be failing considerably in my duty however, if I neglected the opportunity of showing the Urban District Council that their " cast-irou policy "in the matter of the conduct of the Cemetery and Burial aff iirs is often conducive to the keeping of corpses above the ground. As is well known, with po3r people especially, a funeral is a decided expense, and but too often the funds for its pr3p3r carrying out have to be awaited from one or other of the many" burial clubs." This naturally causes delays, and just because the poor p3ople cannot come to the Cemetery C3mmittee office and lay down their fee in hard cash the body has to be lodged for a day and a half longer. Surely there are cases where the Cemetery Committee Officials could relax their cast iron rigidity, especially now that the Council have so decidedly pronounced their wish in the matter; and indeed, unless they do o one sees little hope of the general public doing much in the matter. "First set thine own house in order, and thy neighbour will learn his duty best by example."

Runcorn gethodists have extended to their new Superintendent (the Rev, Alfred Wells), and his assistant minister (the Rev. Barnett Forster) a hearty welcome. They came in the natural order of things to replace two of the finest ministers the Runcorn Circuit has seen. The Rev. C W L Chris- tian (the late Superintendent) was well-known as a sermoniser of a really high order; whilst the Roy. J A B Malvern by his pastoral work, and eloquence as a blunt straightforward gospel advoctra, had Rained the resoect of everyone whs came within his influence. Replacing two such men is naturally no easy task, so that it becomes pleasurable to record that the two new ministers,as preachers at any rate have come up to all expectations, and the laity is so far satisfied that both are worthy and godly men. May they be blessed with health and a happy mission whilst amongst IN. RUNCORN URJAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The above m ntality represented an average death rata of 22 1 Dot 1,090 per annum of the estimated population or 20 Bif the inquest cases were excluded.—ln the corresponding period of last year fticy-six deaths were registered. The number of births registered was fifty-two, as compared with forty-five in Angust 1899. The Chairman observed it was a very satisfactory report: The number of deaths was something like twenty less:than the corresponding month last year, and there was only owe from infectious disease. THE GLASGOW PLAGUE --.I3iNGERS FROM CORPSES AND OVERCROWDING.

The Health Committee recomm !Laded that the Chair- Man of the convnittee and Mr. Jones be empowered to purchase a horse for the Night SAI Department, and the Sanitary Inspector having reported that a nuisance exists at premiFes situated No. 57, Handley-street, Runcorn, arising from such house being overcrowded, it is recommended that a notice be served on the occupier to abate the nuisances within seven days of the service of the notice, and for that purpose to raduce the number of inmates to sk adults and one child, and that in the event of non-compliance with such notice legal proceed- ings be taken. . _ • ' •

The Chairman said there was one matter he had had his attention directed to and that was the outbreak of bubonic plague at Glaggow. Be saw it was reported that it was largely due tut keeping dead bodies too long, and showed them clearly what that practice would lead to if carrird too far. They till had cvves in Runc)rn where it had been alleged corpses had been kept too long. He thought it would be well, considering the result of the practice in Glasgow, if•people would take notice of the matter and use as little delay as plssib!e. Mr. Grine would like to know the position of the Council in the matter in the event of an outbreak. Mr. T. Dean having proposed that the li3alth Commit'cos report be adepted

Mr. Wilson -seconded. Mr. Dean then went oo to allude to the plague. Ile took it that if infection was brouzht by ship the Part Sanitary Authority would deal with it, but if a case or outbreak arose in the to we, unfortunately they would have to deal with it in their own hospital- It showed how careful they ought to be. It would be noticed that in one of the minutes attention was drawn to a cue of overcrowding, and according to what the Chairman had referred to it was clear that the plague in Glaszow had been traceable to overcrowding, or the holding of a " wake" where the people were crowded together. The house had been overpacked. He thought they as a Council should be very particular that they had no cases of overcrowding in the town. No doubt, they would remember he had called the attention of the Sanitary Committee to two or three cases where corpses had been kept too long, and they would also remember that the attention of the public had also been called to the fact that great danger attended the keeping of dead bodies, and he 13,lievel a circular had been sent round asking them no to keep corpses mi long, and if necessary stating they could have the bodies sent to the mortuary. lie dil not think they could be too careful. The Chairman asked Mr Grice would he like the Law- Clerk to explain the position ? Mr. Grine said he would.

Mr. Lake then pointed out that the treatment depen- ded upon whether the case was on hoard ship, or within the district. If on board ship it was a matter for the Port Sanitary Authority, but if it was is a house in the district the Council would have te deal with it them- selvea, Regarding the disposing of dead bodies, their Medical Ofil ler had already power to order the burial of any pe-eori deceased through infect'ous disease, so that the diffi mlty would only arise with other cases. Mr Wiswall added with regard to the reprehensible practice of keeping dead bodies too long, that he was present at the Health Committee meeting where the matter had been discussed. They ail felt that it was dangerous to che public health. Some of the members, however, felt a great timidity about interfering with people, and there was a sentimental objection against pursuing the matter. Still,he thought with due regard to everybody's feelings, they had the public health to consider, and they ciuld see at Glasgow what serious consequence! had been brought about in that direction He did not think that too much nublic attention could he called to the subject, and thought it was understood at the Health Committee meetintg hat the Chairman was to mention the matter. Whether any circulars had been sent out he did not know, but he felt that some good would arise from the ventilation of the subject.
Mr Lake reiterated that the Medical Officer could possibly assist in the matter. The subject then dropped,and the report of the Health Committee) was confirmed.

div.head: LATE MR. JAMES HANDLEY, J.P., 0.0.
div.p: THE LATE MR. JAMES HANDLEY, J.P., 0.0.

Once more it has become our mournful duty says "the Liverpool and District Congregational Magazine." to record the passing away from us of a good and faithful servant of the L3rd. Again too, the loss has come with an unexpected suddenness, and has left a blank in the church, and in many other spheres of public service, which it will be hard to fill. Mr. Handley has for many years been one of the most trusted and beloved leaders in the Garston Church. For more than twenty years he was its Secretary. Being a man of musical taste, be rendered good service in the choir, and for a long time he had been teacher of the senior young men's class in the Sunday school. All who have known Mr. Handley in church work will j3in Mr. Cote in all that he says in his memorial address of the place which the church and its work filled in the life of Mr. Handley. In the con- stancy of his atttandance,the naturalness with which he took upon himself each responsibility and service, as things of course, the simplicity and manifest sincerity of his devotion, it was clear to all, that he was a man with that rich kind of nature which knows that to b 3 " separal'ed from spiritual fellowship is to suffer irreparable loss." But when we pass from church work, and recall the number of public offices hic4 Mr. Handley filled; when we read, as we have just read the number of expressions of loss at his removal, which have come from all kinds of public institutions, together with the remarkably re- presentative character of those who joined in t 38 funeral service, what one feels is that in Mr. Handley we have lost a man who represented that nonconformist ideal of Christian citizenship which we sometimes fear is not so characteristic of us as it formerly was. In business he had prospered. But, as he" bettered his position," he never forgot, or thought of escaping, the responsibilities which attach to it. Mr. Handler's piety was not" sub urban," it made him a servant of all men fur " Christ's sake." He was a hard-working politician. At one time he was chairman of the Garston Liberal Club, and Vice- chairman of the North wich Liberal Association. He was also a member of the Cheshire Cuunty Council and the Garston District Council. For many years he was a member of the old Board of C3ramissioners at Runcorn, and at one time he served as its chairman.

In these and many other ways,Mr. Handley served his generation. And that be did so worthily.bas been made very manifest by the general esteem in which he was held by all classes of the community, as well as by the general expression of sorrow at the loss which the whole community has suffered by his death. The chairman of the Runcorn magisterial bench, an which Mr Handley sat for many years, said of him that " the town had produced no safer guide for any young man to follow than their late friend. He had never known a man so full of energy, and yet withal so devoid of teat: aggressiveness, which sometimes made energy a questionable quality. Mr. Handley was almays at work ; now the trusted c ounseller of a private friend, in whose best interests be would go to any amount of trouble; now the moving spirit in some great commer- cial enterprise; now the public servant, prodigal of his 1 powers for the public good. that court knew him only in his magisterial capacity, and no man ever better qualified himself for that great trust. His conduct of public business and the soundness of his judgment, commanded the re- spect of all, while in the more private duties of the office his great ability and acceracy inspired the admir- ation of his colleagues. He (the chairman) always felt, on these awful occasions, how painfully impotent was anything short of the Divine consolation, but after all, it would be a great co:nfor: t o Mr. Handley's wife and family to realise that his life's work bad been so well doae,' and that he had passed into the ' land of silence ' leaving behind only gracious memories in the minds of his fellow men." As we have already said, Mr. Hendlev's sudden death came with a painful suddenness. On the Friday he was in London on business, on the following Thursday he had entered into rest. The funeral took place on Saturday, 6th August, in the Runcorn cemetery, and was attended by a great concourse of people. The Rev. Thomas Cole c onlucted the service, and delivered the following address : " Met toeether as we are to mourn the death of(' a man greatly beloved,' it is right and fitting that a few words should be said by way of giving expression to our ce nmon sorrow. Having been brought into the most intimate relationship with Mr. Handley, as his minister, for the past twenty years, this duty naturally devolves upo a me. But how am I to discharge it? You will understand me when I sty that at first, I almost despaired of being able to face such a service as this. It is not as if we had been in some measure prepared for the loss we h eve sustained. Had such preparation been granted, we might have recovered from the shock more easily, and the feelings being more under control, my task wile have boon lighter. This blow fell so +suddenly, however, that for a time one felt perfectly dad, and even now I find it hard to newer my balance lam sure that you can appreciate my feelings. You, too, loved him. You, toc, are deeply moved by the sense of a great public less ; and doubt- less I voles your feelings as well as my own when I say that our hearts go out te the stricken widow and sorrowing sons and daughters and relatives in general. And yet;sorrowful though,we are, and natural though it is to give expression to our grief, there is also anottier feeling is us welch struggles for utterance. I have heard many people speak of Mr Handley as one of "nature's gentlemen." said a young man tome on tee day of his death, "but," he continued, " I prefer to call him one of" God's men."' We accept that, not only I as a better description but also as a descriotien more in harmony with our Christian faith. A good men is one of God's best gifts to the world. Hence, how- e eer perplexed and saddened we may be at the dispensation of Gol through the removal of nor friend, if there is one thing more than another that I should like to do to-day it is this—to give expression to our fervent gratitude to God for the man Mr Handley proved himself to be, as s.en in his life and work. He was ' one of God's men.' He was seen to be such in the discharge of his business duties during the entire portion of his life, and still more so in connection with his enultif erious public activities during recent years. ' Whatsoever thy hand fincleth to do, do it wile thy might.' I think that text must often have been in Mr. Handlev's mind. At all events his strenuous and busy life made him a living exemplification of it. But that was not all. Whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lori R 14115 Christ.' That is a still greater principle—the spirit in which a man does his work being of far greater importance than the nature or quantity of the work done. We are con- fident that Mr Handley was always mindful of this. He was a man of strict integrity and upright- ness, and withal be was able by the exercise of great tact to win his way where °there would have failed. _ _ _

Of course I am not here to deal ia extravagances. The best come short of the glory. I would make oo foolish claim on his behalf. But I do say that at bottom he was essentially a religious man—a man who litral 'as under his great Taskrnaster'a eye'—and that is the great thing. Moreover, his religion was marked by great sanity.froa honest te las everlaatingly bandying religious phrases on his lips, the spirit of the Christian faith still pervaded all he said and did. Owing to ample oppor- tunities this feature of his life was especially discernible t 3 same of us. I shall not attempt to address you a' any length on my many years of close asso• ciation with him in church work. Bat you must permit me to say a few words at least. He believed in the institmtion of public worship. Indeed, he so believed in it that I think he tnicsht well have adopted the words of the Psalmist as his own— Lord, I have loved the habitation of Thy house and th, Place where Thine honour dwelleth " And this belief of his had in it no element of superstition. Public worship met a necessity of his nature, and he was profoundly convinced that, separated from spiritual fellowship, a man suffers an irreparable loss. There were times when f r he own sake, sorno of us could have wished that his life had been less active, but, onerous though his dales were, he was rarely absent from his place on la Sanday. Everything connected with chorch life was of interest to him. In the choir an in the Sunday School he was a most dov tted helper. His class in the Sunday School—the senior class of young men—will miss him sorely. Indeed, w- shall all miss him. As the secretary of the church during the whole of mr pastorate, and for several years pr .vious.he brought all his butiness aptitude to boar upon his work. To every good word that I could utter all the officers and members would say Amen. M tch also might be told of his genornsty in the church and out of it. Al! sorts of philanthropic soci,tiee had his sympathy, and as far as it lay in his p ovver to help them I believe he gyre liberally to their auoport. And then how much could be said about him in his home and in the bosom of his family. It can never he too frequently repeated that the home as we know it is the outgrowta of the spirit of the Bible. Wherever the Bible has gone it has Purified and exalted family life. This was the effect of is earliest portions among the Jewish rpople. Under the inflaence of the 0:d Testament Scriptures father ' became a sacred word, woman ' was inveled with dignity, and the 'mother' acquired an influence that made family life a new thing in the world. And the work for which the Old Testament prepared the way was completed br Christ. His presence at the marriage feast of Cana in Galilee, has sanctioned the marriage bond for ever, and now of all the places in the world there is none that is at once so sacred and so glad as the home. How educative of all that is best in human nature ! It was given to 111% as to few, to see how much the home was to Mr. Handley, and haw blessed he was in his family life. But I must desist from saving too much about this. It is too sacred. I men- tion it here partly because it is fitting at such a time as this that we should remem- ber how much we all owe to God for rot - homes, and partly because the sorrow of the widow and family reminds IN of their claim to our sympathy and prayers. The Lord gave, and the Lard bath taken away, blessed he the name of the Lord.' It is easy to utter the first clause of those words. It is not easy at this moment to tatter the second. The stricken widow and family must be profoundly conscious of thia. But we must pray for them, and it may be as they cannot

If ail to realise the divine goodness in the bestowment of the life that was so dear to them, they will yet learn that such goodness must ' order all things well. What we know not n@vy we shall know hereafter.' What bounty is in heaven! May God sanctify to us all this sad dispensation of His providence. Our capacities are not all of the same order, and the work of life Is varied. But day by day, in the world, in the charch, and in the home, God is giving us all opportunities of noble service. Let us not befool ourselves as to what constitutes true life.
We live in deeds, not yesrs ;in thoughts, not breaths ; In feelings. not in figures on a dial; We shoald count time by hesrt throbs ; he most lives Who thinks most, feels the noblest, acts the bast.

To seize each day all the opportunities GA grants us for human service—to accept each day as God's gift for the development and growth of character—to think and speak and act as in the sight of One to whora • we must give an account of our stewardship'—tha is life. That was Christ's view. must work the works of Him that sent Me while it day, the night cometh when no man can work.' Yes, that was Christ's view. And to those who accept it comes the glorious inspiration or 'a hope that maketh not ashamed.' 0 death, where is thy sting? 0 grave, where is tty victory? The sting of death is sin ; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who givech us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.' "

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
Corporation Directors' Report.

The Shin Canal directors of the Manchester Corpera- tion h ,ve drawn up the following report, which they recommend to the Council for adoption :—The past half-year marks an important period in toe hiszory of the canal, particularly having regard to the interests of the Corporation in the undertaking. Alter relAting to the sale of Duke's Dock at Liverpool for £522,000, which enabled the Canal Company to raise a surther capital of over half a million on very favourable terms, as the extra annual expenditure incurred by renting the necessary premises in L'verpool for the conduet of the Bridgewater traffi: has been arranged for at £4,250 a year, the directors express pleasure at the suceessful passage of the Canal Company's Bill through Parliament, by which means the company obtained compulsory powers for the purchase of the racecourse. The question of price would be settled by arbitration. The preliminary works in connection with the ultimate scheme had been comtneneed. The company's receipts for the half-year endure June 30:h, 1900, amounted to £141,346, ae against £121,183 in the corresponding half of 1899, an increase of £17,163. The expenditure showed an increase of £8,588 over the corresponding half of 1899, the fienres being £93,916 for the first half of 1900, ',against £91,358 hi 1899. Tile increase was explained by—the extra cost of coal and materials,which was about £4,200 ; an increase of rents of about £1,100; an apparent increase in the cost of dredging, owing to an abnormal credit in the first half of 1899 for the hire of dredgers; this accounted for about £2,000; and. law and Parliamentary charges in opposing Bills in Parliament, together with rates and taxes,account for over £l,OOO. The receipts from the Bridgewater Depart- ment showed a falling off of £4,098 as compared with the corresponding half of last year, the figures being respectively £21,905 for the half-year ending June, 1899, against £17,807 for the half-year ending June, 1900. toe net result of the half-year's working, after paying the interest on the first and second debentures and surplus land mortgage, left a balance of £16,483 avail- able towards the interest due on the loan of the Man- chester Corporation. The tonnage dealt with during the half-year had been 1,487,841, against 1,325,821 in the corresponding half of last year. The statement of rec3ipts and expenditure for the canal from the date of its opening is as follows : Receipts.
Expenditure - £

1894 ... 97.093 1893 ... 137,474 1896 ... 182,330 1897 ... 204,634 1893 ... 235,336 1899 ... 2'34.775 1900 —. 141.348 (Ist hsl(-year) The gross amount expended on new works was £14,980, the principal items being new workshops at Made Wheel, the completion of roads, railways, and sheds on Corabrook Wharf, and the commencement of the deepening and widening of the berth in connection with it; the remaining items being principally railways and sidings, and preparation of grounds for timber sto rage. The chief engineer of the campany reported that the whole of the property' and plant had been well and efficiently maintained.

The total amount of capital raised by the Manchester Shit) Canal Warehousing Company up to June 1900, was £250,000) entailing an annual rent ef £11,500. At the present time a further sum of £150.000 was being ex- pended Dy the company on the new transit shed on the north side of No. 8 dock, which will cairn the work is completed entail a further annual rent of £7,125. The amount of interest due t • the Manchester Corporation up to June 30:.h, 1930, amounted to £1,131,250. It was intended that on and after January Ist, 1901. ship dues and rents for appropriated berths would be charged, and alao that free towage would be disc 3n- tinned. This should increase the receipts on revenue account next year. As regarded the prospects of the Banal Company for the present half-year, there was no doubt that the abnormal rise in the price of coal would continue to aff act the revenue. There appeared, however, to be every pro meet of the temg ion ttl3 SLIT Canal coa tinning to increase steadily. How the Canal might have Paid. 0 a Sithrday the annual ne ening of the Manchester Liners, L;rnited, was held. Sir Christopher Furness. 1 who presided, made what he admitted was a bold state- ment with regard to the Manchester Ship Canal. Be maintained that it was poisible to have made the I waterway a profitable undertaking. If be had been as 7argely interest:A in the port as he was in anoth u• part of the country, he would have created a firra here with a hundred steamers, costisg four and a half millions of money, which would have traded with the different ports of the world, and that company of 100 steamers would have increased the share value of the Ship Canal by a larger amount than the cost of the steamers. With respect to the business of the Liners. Limited, Sir Christopher went on to say that the rises working of the company haq been successful. They had an actual:balance of £81,134. The directors thought it wise to pursue a conservative policy in dealing with the accounts, and consequently had written £25,000 off for depreciation, and in view of the high premiums to create an insurance fund by transferring £lO.OOO from the profits. They declared a dividend of only 6 per cent whereas the earnings of the year were equal t 3 18 per cent.

A series of meetings for the deepening of the Spiritual Life, similar co those of the well-known Keswick Convention will be held in the above named church from September 16th to 23rd. The meetings will be conducted by the Rev. l 4 T Reed, who has attended the Keswick Convention on seven different occasions. Christians of all deneminations are cordially invited to attend the Bible Readings frem Tuesday to Friday, September ISth to 21st inclusive, and the week night meetings. SUNNIER SALE.—W. T. WiLt.wis is now procaei tug .The whole of the Season's stock to be cleared at a sweeping Reduction." SIN-ic sritEsr AND- LEGII-STREET Warrington.— kdvt Oddfellows' Anniversary. The " Garibaldi Lodge of the National Indepen— ent, Order of 0 ldfello we celebrirel their 39th eniversery on Seturday. The members, accem- paniel by their wives and friends to the numb,T of nearly 60. met at the lodge-house, Blue Lion Ilatel, Nfarket-place, and in three conveyanees journeyed into Cheshire, passing through Walton and Hatton to Stretton, where the party alighted at the Cat and Lion Hotel, the members indulging in the fami- liar game of bowls, while the ladies enjoyed a stroll in the villaree. On re- essembling the drive was continued by a circuitous route to Grappenhall. where another halt was made for a short time,and thence to the lodge-house, which was reached about six o'clock, and where Host Lake had pre- pared a splendid knife and fork tea, to which, after their country drive, all did justice. On the re- moval of the cloth a capital programme of toasts. songs. &c., was gone through. Bro i E Pester oncupied the chair. The toasts were" The Qaeen. and Royal Family" (with musical honours). by pro John Hughes "The Town and Trade of Warring- ton," proposed by Bro A A Horne, and responded to by Bro J Crosby; " The Lodge and Order " proposed by Bro E E Pester, and responded to by the Secretary (Bro T Dickinson) ; and!' The Visiting Brethren," prepesed by Bro T Dickinson, and res- ponded to by Bro J Burgess.(" Friendship" Lodge). The other visiting brethren included Bros Duncan (" Prosperity" Lodge), Hilson and Roberts) ('Per- severance" Lodge), and Warburton and Johnson (" Friendship "Lodge.) Songs, Scce were contribu- ted by Bros. Dickinson, J Hughes, Burgess, Perry, Moss, W Ernson, Roberts, Hilson, Blackshaw, and NicDonald ; also by visitors and ladies. A hearty vote of thanks to the host and hostess brought s very successful anniversary to a Close. OLD FALSE TEETH BOUGHT. Mr. Seutherden looked and saw that the umhrella had not failen and beard semerbing drop on the floor. He found it impos- sible to suit the piisone:s and they left the shop. After tney had gone Mr. Southerden was very uneasy wed certainly felt that he had not been entertaining angels unawares but rather acme undesirabl-, characters. The prisoner Ryan inomedia:ely said she saw some-Wog shining on al, dun near the floor and it turned cm: to be the dress ring which was missing. Mr. Slutherden would he able to tf II the Bench that he s .arcee I the place before he went to the Railway Ste: ion and there was no Hoe on the ledge at that time. There was no doubt that the ring was ban- died in a manner known to • x,:iert thieves ald returned to the lodge. Th. prisone:s refused to give any peitie• -Tact ory scclunt of teemselves,hut from facts which hid coma to his (th 2 Chi,-f Constable's) knowledge, he had reason to believe that they were expert thieves indeed and the cap:izre was one of impertance.—The priainr Il1i;13 said she never had the ling in her hands. If she bad, she would have keet it. St'e wnnld a-k the Bench to be as lenient as possible.—The 'Chairman said the magistrates were convinced that the prisonyrs were ex- 'nere, thieves and they would baclmmitte4 to prison tor two months each.

STOWE Tl'how r. RS I TRourr.c.—Three boys named John wiiiiam Heywood. 8, Garibaldi-street: J inses Ore n street : and ,Pred Burnett, 19, Bostoc,-street, were charged with throwing atones in Saar:bees-lane to the danger of pass"ugers,—D stective Meacock stated that on Wednesday niAt, the n..to of the present month, he was standing war the London and North Western Railway Corn- pany's signal stores when a stone fell near him. A DISGRLCE ro THE ARBLY.—Thomas Rush, a yousig soldier, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street at 10.33 on Friday night.—The Chief Constable stated that prisoner had been in the army live weeks and had been in trouble twice—once for haying been drunk and disorierly in barracks and for threating a non- commissioned offioer. BREACHES or THE FACTORY ACTT3.—Albert Payne, joiner. &amissll-street. was summoned for allowing an apprentice named John Alfred Caldwell to work at his workshop more than seven days without having had him examined by the certifying surgeon as to his fitness, and further with failing to enter his name in the prescribed register.—Mr Sydney Smith, H.M. Inspector of Fictorles. stated that the defend- ant was the occupier of a workshop in Bramhall-street, off Liverpool-road. and the boy was employed by him as an apprentice joiner. He visited the premises on August 15th and found the boy working there. From inquiries made he ascertained that he had not been examined by the surgeon and that his name, Ao., had not been entered in the prescribed register. In the first case he was liab!e to a penalty not exceeding £3, and in the second a penalty not exceeding £2t He had been be:ore that Court twice for similar off snces and had been fined.—Defendant said he left the mater in the bands of his clerk.—The Chairman: But you are responsib'e for your clerk.—Defendant said that such a thing would not happen. apin —He was fined 20s and costs in the first case, and 10s and costs In the second case (23 les in all). NEWSBOYS AS VAGRANTS.—Thomas McLaughlin (17), a newsboy of no settled abode, and Alfred Beckett (17) also a newsboy of no settled abode were charged with having been found sleeping in enclosed press:lige/ in Haydock-street at 1.43 on Monday morning, having no visible means of subsist- ence.—P.S. A MISCHIEVOUS BOY.—John Kay, jun., was summoned for ringing a house door bell in Bold-street to the annoyance of the occunants.—lnspeetor Rowbottorn stated that abont five o'clock on Sunday, August 281 h, he was at Dr. Smith's house in Bold-street when he heard the door bell ring.—The door was opened, and seeing the defendant and another boV running down the street he followed them and obtained de- fendant's name and address. "WOULD NOT WORK.'*—Joseph Heaton was charged with running away from the borough on the first of November, 1899. leavine his two children chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—Mr. B. Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guivcilanie and informed the Bench that the children were first admitted to the Worklime libree years ago last biluary. Tee prisoner had been living apart from his wird and agree I to pay for the maintenance of ths children. He paid for two or three weeks and then left the town. The Guardians pro- secuted him in May 1897 and he was sentenced to a month's Imprisonment. In May 1398 he served a further sit weeks. As he still continued to neglect the children a Warrant Wa3 taken out in 'November 1893 but the prisoner was not apprehended until that morning when ke was arrested in Bolton. The man seemed to have made up his mind not to keep his children.— The Chief Constable said he was informed by Superintendent Monaghan that the prisoner was a man who would not work. He had been before the Court twice for neglect of fatnily.—Mr Shearer said that the children had cost the Union about £sl—The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for three months with hard labour.
THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (in the chair), Mr J Irepherd, and Mr R 'I! Fakelough. _

THRFT OF A Snutr.—Sarah Maloney was- charged with stealing from the dwelling house of John Mc^Joy, 17. Ship- yard, As 5.30 on Wednesday morning a striped cotton shirt value 28 Bd. The facts of the case as related by the Chef Constable, were that the prisoner went to the house of McCoy, who was a forge labourer. on Tuesday evening, and asked to be allowed to sleep there as she had nowhere to go and had no money to pay for lodgings. She was charitably allowed to remain there and lay on the sofa. At five o'clock next morning McCoy returned from work oa the night " shift,' and saw the woman on the sofa. Tho shirt was hanging on the back of a chair. fie retire I to bed, but shortly afterwards in consequence of something his wife said to him, ha got up and round the shirt was missing- Information was given to the police, and It was subsequently ascertained that the shirt had been sold at the shop of Mrs. Gibbons, secon '-hand dealer, of Mersey- street, for fourpence. The prisoner was apprehen led and brought to the Poilos Station and stated that the s•drt belonged to her husband, and she sold it to Mrs. McCoy: She and the prosecutor's wife dra" k the proceeds together, —ltvidence having been given, the magistrates committed he WOMIII GO gaol for seven days.

AN ANTI-v CC rNATIoNIST.—Mo aPs Jon es was summoned for not having his child vaccinated within six months of the data of its birth without giv ng a reasonable excuse.—Mr. Auckland stated that the parents of the child were evidently opposed to vaccination but had not obtained an exemption order. A,SOY TIRE!, SENT TO A REFORM A.TARY.—Leanard Georg Sargent, a 13 year old boy. well-known to the police, was charged with stealing a pair of opera glasses the property of Mrs. Annie Newhy, on the 23rd of A umt. •-Bvidence was taken from which it appeared the boy's parents were alive. but the father a vary respectable mut was often away from home attending to his work.and the boy left to the mother w zs more or less out of hand.
