August,—Complainant stated that he valued his pigeons at 155., and that it was the defendant himself who told him that he had shot the pigeons whilst they were on a neigh- bour's house.—Defeadant said he did not know the pigeons , were Antrobus's, but if they were they were two he had had for 6d.(Laughter).—Complainant stated the pigeons had been given hie:lsm:id he had given dd to the boy that brought them. —The Bench decided that defendant should pay 3s for the i pigeons, and 16s costs. Nox IDENTIFIED.—Heary Ernest Rowlands, of Warrington I was summoned for being the driver of a horse and cart which had no light attached,on the night of the 19th of July. —Defendant pleaded he was not the " defendant."—P.O. Dicken swore that about 23 past ten on the night in question the cart was stopped by him. He saw two persons with it, but could identify neither.—Defendant alleged it was not he, for at the time he had been in Warrington. He also pro- duced a summons from e the Daresbury Police Division for the same offence, which had been served upon him, At Dares- bury the case was dismissed.—P.C. Dicken said he took the name from the cert. and the address was the" Crown Cooperies, Warrington."—The Bench dismissed the case.— - Defendant asked for his expenses—Superintendent Nield remarked as there was no doubt the cart came from the "Crown Cooperies" it would be more the act of an honour- able man if he admitted who was in obarge.—Defendant : I am only in the employ of the Cooperies, but Ido know who was in charge of the cart. -Superintendent Nield : We will summon you to prove the case then; and you will get expenses that tinae.—The Bauch refused to ethic, anything. OTHER OFFENOERS.—Thomas Hughes, 0 Frodsham Lord- ship, for driving without a light through that district, on the 12th of August was fined ss. —He admitted the offence.— Frederick Massey, f ir allowing his dog to stray without col- lar or muzzle, on the 21st of July, WAS fined ss.—James Yar- wood, for being drunk and disorderly was fined ss.—ltobert Dillworth. of Dunliam-o'-th-Mil, was fined the costs 6s 6.1 for allowing his two horses to stray. Defendant said he WAS much obliged to the pence for stabling the horses at the "Horse and Jockey," for when he found they hat got out, they had spent half day looking to' them. He attributed the opening of the gate to the spite of some people whom he had caught" mushrooming" and threatened with the law if theycame again.—Stanley White. another farmer, for allow' inc; nine cattle to stray on the highway. was also fiaed ss. Defendant thought it would be bettpr if the police oaen the gate and sent the cattle back. dergeant Young who proved the eases stated he 1111 been doing that for the last two years without effect. ROWDYISM AT A P 'BLIC-HOTISE.-1-IEAVY FlNE3.—Daniel Garner. and George Midge, of Frodshans.both pleaded guilty to being on licenset premises ant refusing t 3 quit, end also to being drunk and disorderly, on the 25th of August last.— Harry Forster, laadlord of the Cheshire Cheese Inn. Froisham, stated that on the date named he WAS unwell. Whilst lying upstairs he heard a row going on. He also heard his uncle tell the defendants that if they would not make leas noise he would put them out. Illi ige ehallenget him to do So saying he could not put him out. A few minutes after wituess heard a scuffle and went downstairs partly dressed. Illidge had his coat off and Garner was in a fighting attitude and they were making a fearful noise on the step of the house. He telephoned for Sergeant Clays and he came about two minute; later.---Sergeant Clays proved the cases of drunkenness. Midge he had- to lock up and admit to bail the second day. -Garner was dried lOs and 6d costs, or 14 days in the first case, and Midge, against whom Superintendent Nield said there were a large number of previous convictions, was Fined lOs and Ss 6d costs. In the second case Garner was fined 55 and Sa 6d c cite, and Midge 5s and Sc. oosts or seven days.

Barrow open the game and some capital kicking ex- changes were indulged in the best part of the opening being with Barrow, whose forwards were vigorous and good heelers. Ten minutes on, however, Runcorn reached the centre with a rush, and gradually, fought their way into the Barrow twenty-five. Lightfoot, Langley and Walker gained further ground. Faulkner went one better and started a passing movement, This Warder improved and he and Jones getting away, on the right made the pace for all. A try was lost through the latter being unable to take a difficult pass from his consort. Barrow then retaliated and Houghton had to touch down. Play had been some time in mid-field, when it was observed that Runcorn were getting far livelier than their opponents. A succession of rushes looked dangerous and at length Jolley picking up from a scrummage scored a try; the same player failed to add the goal.—At half time Runcorn led by one try, to Barrow nil. WIEW: ‘.14423) On resuming, it was easily seen that Runcorn were likely to come out winners, and excitement was fairly high with the ball continually bobbing about the Barrow uprights. Jolley kicked a penalty goal. Lamonby, Proctor, and Williams did good work for Barrow each effecting fine saves. Getting away on his left,Lamonby raced for Runcorn's line. Houghtcn was in pursuit and so too was Jones. But to the astonishment of all, the Barrow man pushed the international apparently on one side, and showing Jones a clean pair of heels, placed down between the sticks, after a run of three-parts the field. Proctor converted. Runcorn made no more mis• takes after this, and it was not long before they bad a lead again. Houghton scored a penalty goal, and i Faulkner picking up after the Barrow backs had mulled I scored another try. When the end C 3133,1 Runcorn were 10 points (2 goals, 2 tries), to Barrow 5 points (1 goal and 1 try).

div.head: "A" TEAMS COMPEI ITION. Warrington " A " v. Widnes "A."
div.p: "A" TEAMS COMPEI ITION. Warrington " A " v. Widnes "A."

There was a very encouraging attendance at the open- ing match at Wilderspool on Saturday, when the "A " teams of Warrington and Widnes tried conclusions. Neither team was at full strength, and Wariington was exceptionally weak in the back division. The following composed the Warrington team :—Knight, full back ; Jewkes. J Moores. Dickenson, and Pemberton, three- quarters; Smith and R Bate, half backs; Fairhurst. 'to wnseau. Roden, Wiicoa, Boscow, Swift, ,Povey and Skelhorn, forwards. Playing with a slight wind in their favohr, and a bright sun at their backs, the home team bad a distinct advantage in the opening exchanges, but a lack of combination and crude play were accountable for a blank score sheet at half time. Dickenson and Knight were the only players on the Warrington side who did themselve3 justice. Moores throw away a splendid opportunity of opening the home team's scor- ing account by failing to pass to .7ewkes when a few yard 3 from the line. As it was he was collared when trying to score "on his own." Widne3 showed better play in the second half and a forward rush enabled them to score a try—the only point recorded in the match. Warrington made a desperate Effort to draw level in the closing minutes of the match and almost succeeded in doing s,, but wild play at the critical moment spoiled everything. Widnes retire] victors by one try (three point s; to nil.

RUNCORN JUNIORS V. RUNCORN Elornikrs —At Halton. The Hornets started passing movements, but Harrop saved grandly. Rowlands got butt but resumed. From a pass by Rowlands, Morris notched a grand try, and Gadfly scored for the Hornets. In the second half Row- lands gained a try for the Hornets,who won by 11 points to the Juniors' 3 points. LATCHFORD RANGERS v. RUNCORN RECREATION.—At Latcbford on Saturday, Runcorn kicked off against the wind, and a series of scrimmages at the centre followed. Latchford then pressed, but were driven back. The play was very even after, and half time arrived with : Latchford, nil ; Runcorn, nil. Re.startiog. Runcorn got down in the Latchford quarters, and Sutton scored. Barnet kicking a goal. The play now was very unin- teresting, eacn end being visited. Final :—Runcorn Recreation 5 points ; Latchford alums, nil.

E Grestv (Broughton Rangers), and J Platt, hon. secretary (Oldham) were appointiad a sub-committee to carry on the arrangements for the Lancashire v. Yorkshire match at Rochdale. div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
Liverpool and District Amateur League. Earlestown Rovers v. Whiston.

The Rovers made a very encouraging debut under the auspicei of the alywo Lague on Siturday, when they jeurueyed to Whiston to play the club of that ilk. The Robera kicked off, and notwithstanding the tact that they had to face the wind, they had the best of the initial half of the game. The defence however, was too gooi for them and the interval arrived with a blank sheet. With the wind behind them the Rovers had mtttera all their own way and ten minutes after the resumption Rhuebotbam gave them the lead This was immediately followed by another, Broster converting a penalty. Broster also scored a third 'goal and Taylor a flurth, •after which one of the Whiston forwards man- aged to e,core their only point. Final :—Earlestown Rovers, 4 ; Whiston, 1.
LANCASHIRE LEAUUE. Earlestown v. Staleybridge Rovers.

Earleetown opened the season on Saturday with a match at home against Staleybridge Rovers. The visitors were strongly represented their *zeam including Briercliffa and Caok late of Blackburn Rovers. Earlestown had to take the field under a great disadvantage as at the last moment the Rovers objected to Bartley—the homesters cew centre—contending that he played for them two year affo and that he was still on their retaining list, the Earlest.wn Secretary having omitted to obtain his transfer. This was decidedly disappointing to the Earl, stawn executive—And to judge by their remarki— to the homl supporters as well. However the locals had to commoner! wtti., ten men and to continue so for the greater por'...ion of the first half, Clem. Linton only turn ing out to complete the eleven about fiva minutes bafore the interval,.

Chew won the toss and correct to time Monks started on behalf of the Rovers against a stiff breeze and uphill, ia the presence of about 830 spectators. The first move of note came from the visitors' left wing pair but Ba,mher was knocked off the ball by Peaniagton jut as lie was in the act of centering. 'The Rovers forwards were soon in the home half again and after working himself into a nice position Monks crossed to Briercliffe whe however shot yards wide• Materially assisted be the wind, the home. forwards now began to show up a little better and a judicious pass by Clibhorn left Settle with a grand opening. His shot was how( seer luckily charge down by one of the backs and a fruitless corner W4S the only result. Although playing one man short the homesters were finding the Rovers defence plenty to do capital work in the open being nullified by weak and inaccurate shooting. After a brief vieit to the honvi goal Settle and Leach got away on the home left the latter finishing with an excellent shot which Wharton managed to tip over the bar. The ensuing corner was put behind by Morgan. From the goal kick the Rovers forwards raced up the field and Cook was going strongly for goal when he wa.l badly fouled by Heyes within :he I twelve yards line. Toe ensuing penalty was splendidly saved by Che.y. After a seert spell of midfield play , Leach and Settle al an got going and neaty tricking two or three Opponents the former finish' d up with a stiogiue shot ellich struck the uprignt and rebounded into pay. Both teams came within an ace of scoring but the high wind spelled accurate shouting. The in- terval came soon after with neither side having scored. Immediately on reduming the Rovers forced the hemesters to act on the defensive but Chew was quite equal to all the calls made upon him although he had several ticklish shots to deal with. A fine pass;ng rHOVe- ment in which the whole of the visitors forwards par- ticipated looked ote.inous for Earlestown but Clibhorn robbed Briercliffa just as he was in the act of shooting. A m'stake by Green let in Cook who was left with a clear field and had no difficulty in registering the first goal for the Rovers twenty minutes after the resumption. This put new life into the game and both teams fought strentvaidy—one to get on an equality and the other to prevent them. Ten mintres before the cessation Monks put the issue beyond doubt by defeating Chew for the second titme• Although they came very near scoring once or twice the bomesters seemed thoroughly dis heartened after this and the play was very tame and uninteresting to the fioish,tbe Rovers ultim ttely running rue winners by two goals to nil. That the best team won not even the most ardent Earlestown supporter will deny. Of course if Earlestown had taken the field with the frill comolement of players it would have me de a teerzendous difference, as with the wind and hill

behind them they would have made thinga bard for the Rovets. This state of things has been brought about by gross neglect on somebody's part. The player himself says he informed the Etrlestown Secretary that he had previously played for Staleybridge, and the Secretary jusi; as strongly denies this. However, the transfer has been applied for, and is expected to ho ready for to-morrow. The borne backs are not cioite cla.hs enough for the Lancashire League, and this is where the only weakness is. They are far too slow for the smart for- wards opposed to them. The half backs were good enough for any team on SaturJay, Pennington being the pick, although Clibborn played a grand game. The forwards were moderate, the lack of a suitable pivot being sadly felt. F Linton shaped all right, but Bamf ur- long play will not come off in the present company. He does too much kick and a rush, and with good backs to meet the ball this sort of play imyariably falls soft. Morgan wal fair enough, rather on the slo aide, but this can p'rnaps be pat down to temporary stiffness. The Rovers as a whole are a well balanced lot, and they have two capital backs who can kick and tackle splen- didly. Teams : Earlestown : Chew, goal ; Hoye& and Cottam, backs ; Pennington, Green and Clibborn. half hacks ; Morgan, C Linton, F Linton, Leach and Settle, forwards. Staleybridge Rovers : Wharton, goal; Smith and Walton, hacks ; Brown. Johnston, and Lockwood, half backs; BrierclitTe, Cook, Monks, Reed, and Bamber, forwards.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. WARRINGTON BEGIN WELL,
div.p: NORTHERN UNION. WARRINGTON BEGIN WELL,

Ihe c)mpetitien match(); in the Lencisiire section of the Nerthern Union commenced on Saturday. War- ringten's ,ngagement was with Widnes at Widnes, and there was much specnlation as to the result of so impor. taut an encounter b Aween rival teen s Widn-e are always di tilt to boat at home and are generally quite a match for Warrington, but on Saturday tbey had an unpieasant surprise for the visitors won by two tries to one. Warrington were not strongly represented either, for at the last minute almost, Isherwood and Morri.qin cried off, the former; °wine to an injured leg. Hocken. hall and Jee7 filled the vacancies. Widnes turned out as selected, and were welcome] by a crowd of about 4,000 people. Mr. Bruckseaw, Stockport, was the referee, and the teams in his cherge were composed as follows : Warrineton : Hillam, full back; Fish, Hockenhall, La.wleas and Hasria, threequarters ; Duckworth and Bergess, halves ; Taylor, E leo, Swift, B rimer], Mere. weather, Sc witze, A.ndrews.end Jolley, forwards. Weines : Bate', fell hack ; J Huele s. Risoan,Nevitt. and Peacock, thrPeqe arters ; Bewn aryl Deuglas,trelves ; ihnopson, Aspey. Power, Riley, Donnelly, Leyshon. Curtis, an I Allen, forwards. Warringten won the nose and took advantage of a strong brerze in the opP ing half. Asper set the ball rslline, Hallam re turning welnwithin the Widnes' guar' e Burgess got pos-ressi na from the pack but was robbed by Sampson who made for tire Warrington lice, finally panting to Fish who marked safely. Ylereweather removed play to centre by speedy follnwine up, and smart passing by Beree;s, DuTk worth, and Lawless, p it • Widnes on the defeo3ive. Even play followed, until Harris raced up and teckled Biter near the line, the home cestodian b-.ing very slew. Toe Warrington front rank made a rush, but Nevitt saved pluckily. Burgess essayed a droo which failed and Widnes were hard pressed. Bevan (ventually raiscd the siege and by clever play invaded the Warrington half. Nevitt apsis;ed tne movement materiallv, and then the tricky flown secored again and dashed over the line at the corner amid— frantic Widnes cheers. Betsy failed at gee'. This enexpected reverse roused Warring- ton up end they went for the Widnes line with a tremendous rush, Born being the saviour of his side. Operating in the home half Lawless pieked up and by a sm,rt run and punt put the forwar Is oa-side, Hien Enizing the opportunity to score under :he posts. Fish was too eager with the place kick and sent the bail und-r the bar. Bothsides now strove hard for mastery, but Warrington were the stronger,Batey beings weak spot in the home ranks. Dockenhall made a good run to the line but was tackled when he should have passed to Fish A scrimmve folio sied,and Fish receiving smartly dashed in at the nerner, Hallam making a goel att:impt to kick a goal. Warrington kept up the attack ice some time, Lawless and Flockenhall both doing good work, until flown relieved. Widnes made a great effort and reached the Warrin2t rn line, only for Fish to snap uo the ba I and race back to mid-field. Just before rho ietervai Bown hurt his klee h idly, and had to be carried off the field. Half-time : Warrington, 2 tries (6 points) ; Widnes, ene try (3 points). Taylor restarted for Warrington, Widnes putting Aspey wing. and Rispen half in ()lace of Sown. After exchanges Warrington resumed the upper bane and before long L t less intereepted and ran over, only to be brought back for a knock-on. Douglas was held on the home line, but the def-nce prevailed, nil and .Mere• weather both being temperardy laid out. Widnes at. tacked againet rush beiag headed by Hampsoe. Hallam, however, was never at fault and kept them at bay with powerful punts. Widnes next es- sayed a passing run, and made considerable headway, Hue:el however failing to piss Harris at the corner. Warrineton had a warm time of it, Fish finally changing the venue by another brilliant run. He was only secured when he appeared to have the h-me line at his mercy. Burgess and Fish each made vigorous efforts to dash in at close quarters, hut the tackling WAR determined and sure. Then the bdl was whipned along Ito Lawless who ran and passed nicely to Harrir, the wing man mulling the ball with the line at his feet. Hcckenhall came near with a drop and for a time Widnes were very hard pressed. They managed to keep the line intact however, aad were in the Warrington half when the final came with the score unaltered, and Warrington the winners. Runo6rn Beat Barrow.

The opening match at Runcorn took place on Satur- day last, and was patronised by quite a large gathering. During the interval between tast season, and the present one, the local committee have b3en busily engaged. rendering the ground more comfortable to the sight-seer and less dangerous to the player. A largo and commod- ious stand has been erected on the North•ea,t si le ; whilst all around, the rails have been taken further oft the edge of the playing ground, and curved, so as to give more rcorn, and a better sight of the piaying t) all. Naturally much more would have to be accorn. plished to make the Runcorn ground an ideal one ; but, what has been dole, by the Committee has made great improvements and they detp.rve every credit. What is most to the point, hetvevar, just at pre3ent is a brief description of the game. As indicated above Runcorn, (last ytar's first division champions), enter- tained Barrow, (the champions cf the second, Or "A " Division), tor the same period, and the tinsel between them ultimately proved that the difference be-ween both " leagues "is not so surprisingly wide as wculd gener- ally be :unposed. BADEN-POWELL'S INGENUITY. How the Mafeking One Pound Notes
Were Made.
AN INTERVIEW WITH MR. E. J. Rws.

One to! the most interesting forms of currency to a photographer must be the hank noes issued by Colonel Baden-Powell during the siege of Maieking,since thy were made by an amateur photographer in the town, Mr. E. J. ROSS, by a purely photographic process, the ferro-prussiate. Mr. Ross is now in England. We recently had an interview with him, when we had the opportunity of looking over a magnificent collection of photographs taken by him during the siege, trim which we have selected for reproduction a few relating to his manufacture of the notes.

The idea of some such an issue as the Mafeking LI note occurred to Colonel Badet-rowell, when he found that the supply of gold in the town was running short. Knowing Mr. Ross as an amateur photographer, ne con- sulted him upon the feasibility of issuing notes made by photography ; the Colonel, of course, as befitted such an universal genius, providing the design. Mr. Hiss, who has been a resident in the town of Mafeking, for some twelve years, in which, in p %rtner- ship with Mr. Aldred, he carries on an extensive business, had only returned to Mafeking a week before the siege, from the coast where he had beers spending a holiday. He was the possessor of a Tlaoraton-Picaard Ruby camera ; "You know that instrument, no doubt," isesaid to us," a caeital one ; all my photograpos were taken with it. As soon as I saw that there was a prolpect of the siege b3ing a long one, 1 c irefully scoured tle town for plates, and bought all that I could lay my hands on," We were curious enough to enquire what trands he bought.rbut found that they were, without exoeptisn. Ilford. " They were all Words, but of all sorts of speeds and brands from Ordinary to Extra Rapid." Throughout the siege he photographed right and left, and as a result has a record of the entire transaction such as Can hardly be equalled by any other. Knowing Mr. Ross, Colonel Baden Powell disenssed with him his idea of the issue of notes, and to test the practicabi!ity of copying a pea and ink design for th, notes, an experiment was made with the Colonel's sketch book, which Mr. ROSS photographed accordingly. The result of that exposure is to be seen above. The lifelike sketches, including one of a distinctly humorous nature, were readily reproducible. The leaf from the sketch book was a SUCC'M3, and tho next thing to be done was to prepare the deaign. It may not be generally known that the design for the notes themselves was the work of tne popular B.P. We reproduce on page 573 the very first print that was made from the negative used for the notes, together with a finished note itself, countersigned by Captain Greener, and the bank manager, Mr R lirry. Of more immediate interest will be the picture on page 569 This was a trial made from the Colonel's design, when he had got it half flui3hel, ti see how the design that he had started upon would look. A few w nth; now upon the design itself. In the centre is a little Howitzer " Wolf,", made of brass and steel be the railway workmen of Mafeking themselves, while by its side is a pile of home-made four and a half inch shells used in it. Nothing can show more plainly the resources of an educated, skilful man, possessed of willing helpers and just as much knowledge as he has been able to acquire in the intervals of his W:rietly professional study soldiering, than the way in which Mafeking made its own artillery, sh-lls, postage stamps, notes, and other requirements. " Wolf "is only a type of the self-help that was conspicuous all through the siege. Above the Howitzer waves the Uaion Jack, besides which stands a typical member of the Protectorate Regimen% The woman kneeling with the child in her arms symbolises the helpless inhabitants of the town surrounded by those who were prozecting her. Oa the left of the design is the bearded form of one of the loyal Dutch burghers, while on the opposite side is a member of the Town Guard, consp'cuous all through for their gallantry. The design having been found satisfactory so far, was completed, the neeativa made—Mr. Ross used six, one of which got broken by a shell—and printing set in hand. We have already referred to the first print from it.

Silver paper or pletinum would occur to the photo- grapher as a pessible method of printing. There was none to be had, bet the photneraphers of lrlefeking were not to be beaten. With Mr. Ross was associated Captain Greener, the chief paymaster, and this officer, whose portrait we give on page 572, bethought himself of the ferro-prussiate proasss. No time was lost, the directions and formula were laureed up in an old text book, and the preliminary trials made. Needless to say, they were successful, and the Mefeking notes are blue prints. roe materials required, as our readers know, are potassium ferrieyanide (red prussiate of potash) and ammonio- citrate of iron. The piussiate was plentiful enough, but the supply of ammonio-citrate of iron was a very limited one. The whole of what was in the town was speedily used up, but some more was brought—in a little pot— from the north, by a flatly- runner, and this had to last for the rest of the Beige. The paper used in making the notes was ordinary note paper, of which there was a plentiful supply. Every night Captain Greener coated the paper for the next day's printing, brushing the sensitising solution on with a camel-hair brush, and allowing it to dry till the morning, when till pri:it3 were made by Mr. Ross. In the brilliant tight of the South African sun, the print- ing itself took very little time, most of the prints being knocked off in from fifteen to twenty minutes. The printing quality ot the various neeativee, as might be expected when one considers the difficulties under which they were m ide, varied considerehly. Everything in Mafeking was done light heartedly, and the very uegatives themselves were nicknamed according to the speed wirh which they performed their work The cleve,t wed best was known as" The Fiigh Velocity, Quick Firer," one which toek an intermediate time— can ohs be the" average negative "of the textbooks of which we hear si much, but never see ?—was christened the " Arinsrring Gun," whilst the shwt,at printer of the lot bore the title of this "Lord Nelson Muzzle Loader." " Were you ever in any risk from the tire ?" we pequired. " I was never actually wounded " was the repiy, "but came very near it once or twice, while engaged in meeting the notes. One morning a shell dropped into our auction room not more than fifteen Daces from the dug-out, and blew the room all to pieces I was Aandinvat tho top of the ladder leading to the _
dtiwout,and was knocked head over heeis to ti-t-t; bottom.

Another time, one of the negatives was smashed by a piece of shrapnel. There was a good deal of difficulty at first in getting the paper evenly coated. Clot am Greener had never worked the ferro-prussiate process before, but after a little practice the blotches and uneven patches dis- appeared, and in the not,s that we saw the background was uniform and smooth.

One serious difficulty, however, was continuous right through the siege. The Eunply of good water, rain water was what Mr. Ross particularly wanted, was an extremely limited one, and it was only by stealth that sufficient for his photographic purposes could be obtained. Dad the quantity tuat he was consuming on this score only have leaked out, his photographic per- formances might have come to a very abrupt termina- tion. As it was, he Eucceeded in covering them with a veil of obscurity, and, although the supply of sufficient rain water was never easy,yet he managed to get enough for his immediate requirements all the time. The Mafeking Mint, was situate at the back of his business premises. In this dug-out, a subterranean dark room of a most uninviting charac- ter, with nothing but its bomb-proof nature to recommend it, we see M. Ross himself washing out the notes. As our readers will know well, when ferre- prussiate is employed, this is the only process necessary after printing, Banging up befera the photographer are a row of the notes drying. Here in this dug-out, surely some of the strangest cir- cumstances under which an amateur photographer ever worked, Mr. Ross produc( d the bank notes at the rate of about twenty a day, until before the edge terminated over five hundred of them had been issued.

It is worth mentioning that, a 3 a business speculation, the issue of notes may be regarded as distinctly a sue- c-ss. They were exchanged for a sovereign in gold,and ro7. one has ever been presented for repayment, the ex- planation being, of course, that the Mafeking Beige note is worth a good deal more than its face value. The appearance of the dug-out from the outside is seen in another of the picturt?s, which we are privileged to reproduce. The inscription "No Admittance" on the board of the" Mafeking Mint," it was explained, was regarded by most friends as a joke, the formula tieing. " Well, if there is no admittance, I'm going in," The other figure in this group is Captain Greener, who offi- ciated not only as paper sensitiser, and superintendent of the mint generally, but in his capacity of paymaster had to countersign every note before it was issued. Amongst Mr. Ross's collectioa of these notes is one which was not issued ,and has been marked "cancelled." It is one of a batch which caused them some annoy- ance. Spending one night bard at work. sensitisine paper, they found in the morning when starting to prict that, although it li d not been noticed beforn, they had been using, insteof plain note paper,the official paper of the BechuanalatO Border Police, and that embossed on every sheet weri. tne initials of the force "8.8. P. surmounted by a erown. The notes were therefore not issued.—Froria " Photography."

WARRINGTON. The Fancy Dress Parade and Carnival. The result of the fancy dress cycle parade and carnival, in aid of the Infirmary, must be considered eminently satisfactory by the promoters. ill acknowledging the services of one of the collectors, Mr. Picka.vance, the secretary, says :—" so far as we are able to make out the total proceeds ana"nt: to something like £.3so—not so bad for such a small and not over-rich town—made up as follows : Street collection over £l7O. concert £3O, book Col- -IPctions about £BO, watch competition between £BO and.Eloo."
Fire in Bridge-street.

At about 9.30 on Monday evening a fire broke oat on the pr•Atnises of John Moginn, furniture dealer and piano and sewing machine agent, Bridge" street. It appears that Mrs. Elizabeth Little, villa of Benjamin Little, who is the manager for Messrs Scale, boot and shoo dealers, observed flames. issuing from the third storey of the premises occupied by Mr. Maginn as a warehouse, and she immediately informed Mrs. Maginn who telephoned to the Fire Engine Station. At 945 the Fire Brigade under the direction of Deputy Superin- tendent. Turner, tarnel out with the reel and hoses, but the fire was not extinguished until. 11.30. The premises contained a large number ot sewitig machines, bedroom and sitting room suites, bedsteads and other furniture and considerable damage was caused by the fire and water. Harry Vane a youth employed by Mr Maginn states that he was the last person to leave the warehouse, and when he did so everything appeared to be right. The origin of the fire is unknown. The damage is covered by insurance.

div.head: ALLEGED SHOOTING OUTRAGE AT
div.p: ALLEGED SHOOTING OUTRAGE AT
APPLETON•
A Boy Shot in the Leg and Mouth;

At the Warrialton Occasional Court on Wednesiay morning, before Mr. Tinzley, Thomas Gregsan, teams - man, in the employ of Mr. Yarwood. Applona, was charged with unlawfully and maliciously firing a gun at a boy named Colin Bennett.. on Mr. Yarwool's farm, at six o'clock on Tuesday °Visaing, with intent to do him grevous bodily harm. C•implainant, who lives in Gaskell-street, Stockton Heath, said oe !viz his work at Me3Sr3. Fletcher Russell's works at four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon and went to Mr Yarwoecfs farm at Appleton to help the milk boy. He met prisoner, and had a short canversatien with him. Prisoner struck another boy, whereupon they all (there'were three of them) ran away, followed by the prisoner, who had a stick. He however, failed to catch them and one of the boys went back to bring his j acket The prisoner seeing them wont into the stable and brought out a gun, which he fired at them. He (wit- ness) was shot in the leg and mouth and fell on his face.—By prisoner : On Sunday prisoner struck bira with a stick and threw a stone at him. He did not call him names. Another boy called prisoner a coward. 13,!rt Howells, a boy, living at Latchford, said he work,d a: the farm, and at the time mentioned he wa with Beenett. He was working and took a brush, for use, out of the stable, and when he was returning with it prisoner accosted him and called him names for using it. Prisoner struek him twice with the brush, and a libaurer named Martin Malone took the brush off hirn. Ss irtly afterwards prisoner chased them widi a etick • and failing to catch them brought the gun out. He pointed it at Bennett and fired twice. Martin Malone, a labourer, also employed at the farm, said he was in the stable when prisoner went in for the gun. He saw him put two cartridges in it and go out. A minute afterwards he hoard the gun fired. Prisoner had been aggravated to some extent by the boys. P.C. 13.. lime, stationed at Stockton Heath, said he received information at the Police Station from Bennett at 6.40 on Tuesday evening about the matter and went to the farm, where he arrested the prisoner. When charged he said " I fired, and the shot went up into the air." PriFoner now said he was under the influence of drink at the tine. He was remanded until Tuesday next.

A WARRINGTON SOY'S SHOCKING DEATH.
Killed by a Falling Stone.

A coroner's inquiry was opened in toe Police Station, Warrington, on Monday afternoon, relative to the death of a ellitd, four ye tra of age named Ernest Jones, son of Mr. Arthur Jones, of Liverpol-riad, who was killed opposite his home on Saturday afternoon by the fah of a huge slab of stone, weighing nearly half a ton. A new puelie convenience is toeing erected close to the Bowling Green Inn and the old one taken down. Ths stone , which fell on the child was one which had been :eft standing with very little support. rho boy's head was crushed in a shocking manner between the stone and a pile of pressed brieka on which he was pl tying at the time. Mr. Brighouse was the coroner, and Mr. Barton, foreman of the jury. Mr. A, Browne appeared for the I father of the deceased. Me. Stanley Wilson (deputy ITown Cl-rk) for the Corporation; and Mr C. EL Unsworth I for Mr Harry FAirc'ough,the contractor. Mr George Clay (Williams and Clay) and 3 Mr James Deas, the bborougo sanitary engineer, were also prtsent. Supsrintendent Monaghan watched the inquiry on behalf of the police. The Csroner remarked to the solicitors that they must not use the witnesses for the purpose of finding out who was to blame. If be (the coroner) found that any one was to blame criminally he was going to stop the inquiry. They were not going to travel into the realms ot civil 1 ;ability. Arthur Jones, blacksmith, 32, Uverpool-road, said the deceased was his son, and was four years of age. He last saw him alive at half—past ten on Saturday morning, In the evening he was out and was toll by a gentleman that a serious accident had happened to his son. He afterwards saw him dead. Lie welt to the place where the accident happened. A new public urinal was to be erected, and the rtti one was bdng pulled down. One, of the stones of the old winal had been left standing. It was six feet e'ght inenes high, four feet three inches wide, four and a half indica thick, and had been five inches in the ground. In answer to the Coroner, - -

Mr. Unsworth stated that Mr. Falcolough had under- taken the work on behalf of tip, Carpiration by contract. A juror asked if the Contract had not been sub-let Co Messrs. Williams and Clay ? The Corcn-r said the jury only wanted to know who was the particular individual who had charge of toe work, and having found that out the: would have to ascbrtain if that individual took prop:T c ire or not, and whether there was criminal negligence or not. Mr. Unsworth asked the witness wh ther he noticed any cement on the bottom of the slab. Witn.ss sad he did not. le t,,re was cement it did not hold. The workmen had nit been near the place bince Friday he was told. Toe vibration of pis Sing car:s and omnibuses bad made the stone fall. The Coroner said they would get ou b tter if they had the person who had charge of the work. In answer to a question by the Coroner, _ _

Mr.-Clay said his firm had a sub-contract, but /lad nothing whatever to do with the stone which had falleh. He handed to the Coroner a statement of the verbal in- structions he reoetved from Mr. F.iirclough. Mr. Clay'a son stated that they had cold one of Mr. Fairc'ough's meu that the stone na.ci bette: be t.*lten down.

Mr Wilson handed to the Coroner rs copy of the speci- fication between the Grrporation and Mr Faircloug b. The Coroner read the following from it :--" The con- tractor must take all risks of the old and new property, and of life and limb of workmen, pedestrians or other persons, and muss take prcper steps to ensure the safety of such." _ _
The Coroner asked what was to bo done with the stone?

Mr Deas said it was to forma part of the new erection; Mr Wilson obselv3d that it bad t, ba worked up into another pogition. ' The Coroner: Wa3 it standing in its original p)sition? Mr Browne: It was.
Ths Coroner °Nerved that it was not fair to 1.9,1 into the matter in Mr Fairelough's absence, and the inquEst as a. j ;urned until Tuesday morning tux%

div.head: CYCLIST WEDDING AT GREAT
div.p: CYCLIST WEDDING AT GREAT
SAN KEY.

A wedding on somewhat novel lines was so'emn- ized at Sr. Mary's Churcb,Cireet Sankey, last Thurs- day, the contracting parties being Mr W 11 Ireland, and Lily, the eldest daughter of Mr W A Bingham, of Tower View, ()refit Sankey. The bridegroom,who is well known,and popular in the vicinity, is a cycle macutfotrirer, but it is in connection with his sing- ing abilities that he is more widely known, in Warringto i and district. The party met at the house ft le bride, and proceeded to the church on c7cles, bele.: met at the church by the bridegroom, who also cycled thither, Mr S Hodgson, of Widnes, officiated as best man,and Miss .Ndie Bingham,sister of the bride, and Miss Dinah Ireland, sister of the bridegroom were the bridesmaids. The Rev J R Jones performed the ceremony. The wedding. bad been much talked of, and drew a large number of spectators. eager to witness thenovel sight. The ladies wore very pretty costumes, consisting of cream ycling skirts with silk bodices trimmed with lace and they also wore white sailor hats. They carried their bouquets affixed to the bicycles with white streamers. The bridegroom was attired in a neat cycling suit and a number of cyclists were present in church. The party afterwards cycled to the St. Mary's Schools where the wedding breakfast was served. Numerous presents were;received and they were on view in the schoolroom.
Daresbury .Sunday_Schoot Trip.

The scholars attending tne Church. Sunday Sch ools of Moore, Hatton, Preston Brook and Daresbury were given their annual summer outing on Friday afternoon, when about 133 scholars with their teachers and about 40 parents were conveyed in 'buses to Mersey Viev-r,Froclsbam. The party reached the summit of the hill a little after three, having enjoyed the drive very much. Amusements occupied the time until tea was partaken of in the large re- freshment room, after which donkey riding and other games were indulged in until the time came when a start for home had to be made. The fol- lowing teachers accompanied the party :—The Rev H 'I? Clerk, Mrs Clark, Misses Groome, Darlington, Horrabin, Hamblen, Green, Wright, Bennett, Houghton and Dunbabin, and Mrs Whitlow. Despite the rain which unfortunately commenced before leaving Frothham, the outing was much en- , j9yed.

Signor Piccolomini—An Appeal.

Sir,—May I enlist the sympathies of your readers for the composer of so many beautiful songs. Signor H. Paulet Piccolomini, who has lost memory and brain power, and who, it is feared, will never be able to create another of his charming melodies ? His sad state has nem caused by long-continued ill- health and monetary difficulties. Consequently his wife and children have nothing for their maintenance but a small sum which has been collected for them, which is totally inadequate to their needs. For the composer of "Ora Pro Nobis," " Whisper and I shall hear," and a hundred sweet songs lask those who have enjoyed his work to give as their hearts dictate. Offerings sent to me shall be forwardel to Madame Fiecolomini.—Yours, G. HUBI NEWCOMBE. Penketh, Warrington, S,ptember Ist.
LATEST NEWS.
CHINA.
The Allies in the Forbidden City,

The Secretary for India on Wednesday received the following telegram from Sir A • Gaselee, dated Pekin, 29th August "Allied troops marshed through the Forbidden City yesterday. Each army represented in propor- tion to strength. "The British took the third place in the proces- sion, Russians and Japanese being in much greater j strength. " We were represented by detachments of all ; corps, ageregaticg 400 men. The salute was fired by our artillery." -
Swimming Across the Channel.
The Lady Fails in her Attempt.

A telegram from Calais received at Dover y ester day announces that Madame Icacescu failed in her attempt to swim across the English Channel yesterday. After a remarkable swim of nearly 20 miles the lady gave up. and was taken on board the tug that was following her. Madame von Icacescu left for Paris. She will probably make another attempt next week if the weather conditions are favourable.

div.p: Disaster on a Steamer.
A boiler burst yesterday on the Servian steamer Aegotin on the Danube. Captain and twelve men were drowned.

The Hastings Festival. North v. South. Delightful weather pre- vailed, and a large company had assembled at noon, but owing to the late arrival of the train a stut could not be made until 12.40. LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Ladybrand Relieved. Sharp Artillery Fight. Maseru. WEDNESDAY.

On evacuating Ladybrand the Boer; left a rear- guard on Platburg. In the course of the morning both British and Boer artillery came into action. The Boers eventually retired, leaving both the mountain and town in our possession. The stores in the town were cleared of the greater part of their contents.
Cape Town, THURSDAY, 10.10 a.m.

It is now confirmed that Ladybrand was relieved on Tuesday. The total British casualties were five wounded. The seige was entirely uneventful, but it forcibly indicates the activity of the Free State commandos.

div.head: Home.
div.p: Home.
CAPETOWN, WEDNESDAY. There are encouraging signs of the near approach

of the end of the war. The personnel of the army transport in Orange River Colony has been paid off and disbanded, and the Imperial Yeomanry and scouts employed in that country have arrived at Capetown, also with the aject of receiving their final pay. Four of Lord Roberts's chargers have arrived here.
Major-GeneTal Baden-Powell will arrive here to- morrow.

Death of Captain Plomer. Captain Alfred Durham Plomer, who was reported by Lord Roberts as wounded and captured in Butler's action near Geluk on Thursday, August 2.3, and is now repor- ted by released British prisonsrs to have died of his wounds at Nooitgedacht, joined the regiment as second lieutenant on March 23, 1889, being promo"ed to lieutenant August 11, 1890. and captain July 9.7, 1896. Prior to the outbreak of the war he was stationed with the devot of his regiment at Warrington. He had no previous war service. The news of his death occasioned consider Able reel, t in Warrington, where he was highly respected. Captain Plomer was well-known in cricketing circles in Lanes- shire, and for many years was attached to the Warring- ton Club, where be first made his appearance in 1894. When stationed at Orford Barracks he was a regular playing member of the Warrington first team. Last season he played for Warrington in several matches, but latterly be cast in his lot with the Western Club. whose ground is situate at Eccles. In 1895 he was drafted to the depot at Cork, and when he returned to Orford Barracks he was appointed adjutant. On the outbreak of the war he volunteered for active service, but his request was not granted until February 25, on which day he left Warrington with a detachmeht of the Ist King's Liverpool Regiment.

Driver J. Whitley's Exciting Experiences.

The Obstinancy of the American Mules. Driver James Wnitley. M Battery, Roeal Horae Artil- lery, has sent an interesting letter to his brother who resides at Stockton Heath. In it he says :—"Since I last wrote lam glad to say that I have kept in the best of , health. We have, since leaving Bloemfontein, changed our horses for mules and we were ordered to compose a part of the flying or relief column, for the relief of Mafeking. We travelled almost night aad day to that place doing a record march—about 300 miles in twelve days. There were twelve mules to each waggon or gun and two drivers. I had charge of five and my mate also had five. We ride the leader and drive from the waggon or gun, with long reins and a whip. We have some floe sport with the animals at times but on the whole they are quite easy to drive. When we got in Mafeking Baden-Powell congratulated us upon our march and told us that it would live in history for years to come- He also com- plimented Colonel Mahon on commanding such a splendid body of men. I am in good trim and fine health. I shall never forget the joy of the people in Mafeking when they heard the report of our guns outside the town. The men got on the tops of the houses and other buildings te get the first sight of the relief column coming. The Boers fled from us in all directions. Their encampments,which were packed, were cleared in about twenty minutes." Writing later Driver Whitley narrates his experiences on the march from Bloemfontein to Pretoria. He says:— "We had a very long march on May Ist to Barkley West. I bad five mules on that march, and nice things they oare too. They are ten times worse than donkeys. We had American mu'es which proved to be very good as regards " sticking " the roads and marching but they are very obstinate when they are unhooked. I will just give you an instance of what happened one night when I was on picket duty. Mules get loose and eat their reins with which they are tied up. We had one vicious mule and that got loose. I thought I had got it when all at once, to my surprise, I found it was dodging me round a waggon. I kept walking round the waggon and the mule did likewise. I kept this up for some time and then I walked in the opposite direction thinking I would get it that way but it was too artful. It was watching me. At last I got about three more men to help ma, and then we managed to get it after a hard struggle. At Fourteen Streams the bridges were blown up, so the column had to ford the river, When it came to our turn with the mules we had a very awkward struggle, as mules don't like eatning water. I was going along very nicely until we got in the centre of the river, when all at Once the waggon in front of me go.'; stuck in the bed of the river. I had to pass on the left of it, but unfortunately I got stuck myself, there being some very big rocks in the bed of the river. My mules were w,ruggling very hard to get to the other side but it wee impossible for them to get across. The mule that I WAS riding, struggled so hard that it came down in the water and of course that meant me as well. I was in a nice pickle for about two hours, and the only man that came to my assistance was our warrant officer, who, I call a very brave man and a gentleman as he was the means of getting me out. Without his aid I dou'a think I could have managed to have pulled through. IVe entered the Transvaal on May 15th and kept on marching and fight- ing ' our way to Johannesburg and then to Pretoria, arriving there on July Bth. At present lam encamped in Pretoria awaiting orders to go elsewhere under General Hunter. We have just been to Brock he; Spruit and we have got two guos in a good position on the Kopjes there. I have just seen three hundred dead bullocks, mules and horses, and owing to the exoosure they are a horrible sight, and there is a fearful smell. If I don't get drafted off to China from here I hope to be at home before Christmas."

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

A strong draft of non-commissioned officers and men of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regi- ment with headquarters at Warrington will next week go to South Africa to reinforce the battilion. The draft is to go out in the steamship Oro Tabs which is timed to leave Southampton for Cspetown on 'y ednesday. Major Brookes, Liverpool Regiment, has retired from the service. He was only re-appointed to the Liverpool Regiment from half pay last March. Captain Glynn has been promoted .iajor in the Liverpool Regiment to fill the vacancy, lie j)ined the regiment from the militia in 1885; was adjutant of his battalion from 1888 to 1892, and became cap- tain in 1891. Major Glynn is now employed on special service in South Africa. Second Lieutenants Hanbury, Conran, Cattell, Gordon, Wit:lBer, Spooner, and Clarkson, of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, have been promoted to the rank of Lieutenant in the Corps. Lieutenant Hanbury joined the battalion in Novem- ber, 1893; Lieutant Conran in March, 1599; Lieu- tenant Cattell last October; Lieutenant Gordon in INovember ; Lieutenants Winer and Spooner in December, and Lieutenant Clarkson was gazetted to the C3rp3 last January. Tney are all serving in South Africa with the battalion,and are smart young officers. .
Captain Evans Lambe, 2arl Bittalinn High- land L 1., has been appointed to the staff of Iklajor General Swaine as Inspector of muskdtry in this district. _ .

_ ... Major Nicholls second in command of the 4th battalion Cheshire Re2iment, has been granted the honorary rank of Lieutenant-Colonel on completing the qualifying period of 20 years' service. Lieutenant the Duke ef Virestminsr. Cheshire Yeomanry,who has on the recommendation of Lord Roberts been given a commission as Second Lieu- tenant in the Royal Horse Guards,will not however join that regiment just yet but will continue his present employment as aide de camp to Sir A Milner. The Duke has been less than two years an officer of the Cheshire Yeomanry for he was ap- pointPd Second Lieutenant in the Corps in Novem- ber 1898.
Good Templary.

. . The usual weekly meeting of the " Young ilii9- Bioll of Warrington "Juvenile Temple was held on Wednesday evening in the Brick-street schoolroom. Sister S L Sheath, C.T., opened the meeting, and seven new members were proposed and initiated. The following programme was then given by the children :—Dialogue, "Onty a medicine," Sisters S L Sheath, J Walton, M Shaw, and F Plucknett ; recit- ation, "Battle of Bannockburn," Bro. Howarth; dialogue,l' The Idle shepherd-boy," Sisters N Walt on and Dean; glee," Victoria," Sisters J Walton, M Dean, Bebbington, 11 Shaw, S L Sheath, and F Plucknett. Bro Roberts then spoke a few words of encouragement to the children, after which the lodge was cloaed.—The meeting of the adult lodge was afterwards held in the same room, Bro Roberts C.T., presiding. Visitors were present from the Star of the East" Lodge," Warrington. Two new mem- bers were initiated into the lodge.

Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds Warrington District. The Iran Workers Home Lodge held its quarterly meeting at the "Rope and Anchor" Buttermarket- street, Bro II Warburton WM. P.P.S.S. in the chair, and T Lecknesby DM. in the vice chair. The Secre- tary Bro D Harris, having read the statement of acc3unts which showed a substantial gain for the quarter, the Chairman said he had a very piea•ing duty before him that evening. In the first place he wished the district officers a very hearty welcome. Secondly, he wished to draw their attention to the splendid set of regalia purchased voluntarily by the Lodge members. The Chairman then called upon Pro. C.S. Miller to present the regalia to the Lodge officials. Pro. C.S. Miller, on rising. said he did not come prepared, as he had no idea of the Chairman's intention of calling on him that evening. However, he should endeavour to the best of his ability to comply with the Chairman's wish. It was the first time he had been called upon to make a presentation of this kind. The regalia was indeed very beautiful, and was a credit to the Lodge members. He then in a few well chosen words of advice and counsel, presented the regalia to the Lodge officers amidst a round of applause. Pro. D.C. Haley, P.P.C.S. Massey, and Hall also addressed the meeting. The Chairman, Bro. 11. Warburton rose on behalf of the lodge to thank Bro C S Miller for his kind remarks to the lodge and the happy manner in which he presented the rega- lia. He also wished to propose a very hearty vote of thanks to the district officers for their attendance and advice during the evening which he coula tell them was very much apnreciated by the assembled members. (Applause.) The Secretary Bro D Harris, in seconding the vote of thanks, said he could only add his te4timony to that of their chairman. The discrict officers were always welcome. The officers briefly responded, after which the evening was brought to a close.

I hasten to make this pleasing statement of fact while there is opportunity, for later in the season a change may twit) ohm o'er the nene. Lt U 3 hope it will not be yet, for W4rrin ;ton coeti da very well with a run of success like Runcorn had last slaslrt, and rtv.thinks thy have got as good a team. Last Saturday they astonished their warmest admirers by whacking :Widnes at Widnes, and with a team too, considerably below par," Snuck" Bate, Isherwood.and Morrison all being absentees. But " needs must when the d- drives "and wd won no:lwithstandinz the s!veritF of the handicap. Two points are very welcome at this stage of the competition. Ocher folks can go there for summer holidays and physical recuperatioa if they bk —and if their relatives have not consigned them to Rainhill beforehand—but the prospect does not appeal to me. It's a foul smelling place, and if the football ground were nearer the centre of the town Widnes would win oftener, unless other clubs tumbled to the cause and sent their players for a week's inolulation prior to the match. Out at Lowerhouse-lane, however, you got quite a healthy breze. and all the conditiona were well suited to football. div.head: DEATH OF MISS BIRCHALL.
div.p: THE DEATH OF MISS BIRCHALL.

At St. Helens Town flail. on Monday, Mr. S. Brig- Whist!, county c n*oner, held an inqaest on the body of Mary Alice Birchall, single woman,aged 26, of 14,Harris- Areet, whose body was found in the Leg of Mutton dam near Taylor Park, on Saturday morning, after she had bees missing from home four days. Mr. -Tosenh Birchall, anetioneer, of New Market-place, St. Helens, said deceased a ;Led as his clerk. He last saw her at a cparter to five on Tuesday night. She had been low- spirited since her mother died six months ago, and she diFappeared exactly six months tothe date of the funeral of her mo'her. When he loft her at the office she had several accounts to deal with, and he found that she had balanced up the books and made everything right. She had bnween £2O and £3O to deal with, and everything was perfectly straight. She had never been the same girl since hr mother died, but he had not found any letter or anything from her.—Miss Hien Birchall, sister, said that on Tuesday night her sister appeared all right. She asked her to go with her to a meeting, but she declined, and said she was expect- ing a friend. Witness returned home at twenty minutes to ten, when deceased had gene.—Detective Holding said that on Friday afternoon the police received information that Mr Sine_tham, the keeper of Taylor Park, had found a hat in the Leg of Mutton dam, and it was identified as that of Miss Birchall. They recovered the body on Saturday. The place would be about a mile and a quarter from her home. Testimonial to Mr. Shirley. A mseting of this Council was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Moniay W Collingwood J. P., Presided, and there were also present :—Messrs C B F Barron, W Thompson, N Siddeley, W Gilmour, J Simpson, Dr Patterson, J Fitzgerald, T Ormand, With W W Sairley (clerk), A Bowes (surveyor), D H Lloyd (gas engineer.) GRAVE DIGGERS AND TEIEIR WAGES. At a meeting of the Cemetery Committee, letters dated August 14th were read from George Day and WilHem Day, grave diggers at the Cemetery, applying for an advance of waves, after consideration of which, it was resolved that G rerge Day, being in receipt of 51 per hour, his wages be not increased ; and William Dty be increased from 411 to 5 1 per hour.—The Clerk reported that the Lord Beitiop of Liverpool had. on Friday, the 17ch of August, in compliance with the petition of this Cmucil, attended at the Cemetery, and consecrated an additional Vol of land as a burial ground. accerdine to the rites of the Church of England. It svit resolved that the aleoeetioe of the several prices of the additional plot of land referred to be referred to a sub-committee con- sisting of Councillors Simpson, Ormand, Thompson, Patterson, and Siddeley, , and that the same sub-commit- tee report generally upon any other matters at the Cemetery reqairing attention ; and also that tenders be invited for repairs to the roof of the Cemetery Chapel end referred to the subeeemenittee named in the forego- ing resolution, with poor to 'accept the same. Mr. Simpeot prooosnd and Mr. Siddeley seconded the adoption of the minutes, which were agreed to. TECHNICAL INSPRUC,TION COMMITTEE. A circuler letter dated the 13th of Aueuet, was read before this Committee from the Lancashire County Council, stating that the Technical Instruction Corn- mi,tee had recommended a grant of a sum not exceeding £l6O to the Newton-in-vtakerfield Urban District Cenncil in aid of Technical Instruction for the year 1900 and 1901, whereupon it was resolved that the offer of the leeneasleire County Council be a,ncepted. GAS COMMITTEE. The Eogineer'e !monthly report was read, front which it appeared that one of Her Mejesty's Inspeetors had been at the Gas Works that day, and condemned the sulphate of ammonia plant. It was resolved that the Clerk write to the Inspector and inform him that the Council had, prior to his visit, already decided to aban- don the plant, an 1 had invited estitnetes for an entirely new plant.-3 letter dtted the 26th July, was read from Mr. A. C. Leslie, agent to the Rlght Hon. Lerd Newton, stating that he could not consent to the Council's pro' peal to carry gas pipes through the arches over Newton Brook unlese the Council would undertake not only to restore the structure of the bridge, but, also, to keep the bridge in repair tor the future, and take all risk of eereege to the pines from traffic over the bridgi. After consideration of which, it Wa7 resolved that the Eegineer be inetructed to draw up an alternative scheme which would avoid, if possible, the necessity of interfering with the structure of the bridge' At a further meeting of the committee held on Monday afternoon las', the engineer sub mitted an alternative uheme far carrying tee gas mei!: across Newton Brook, After c insideration it was resolved that subject to the approval of L ne, Ne•ton, the alteenative plan now sub- mitted be adopted. The minute 3 were c onfirmed on the proposition of Mr. Tb empson.

THE NEW WATER SUPPLY. TO BE TURNED ON NEX C WEEK. Mr. Ber-en move i the aleptioe of the minute.; of the Water C oumittee which did not centeirt auything of pale lic interest. Mr. Thempsen cended. There was a number of small matters to attend to bat he thought that by next week the water would b' terned on. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Garneur said the answer was very eetiefae.tory. HIGHWAYS AND SANITARY COMM P fEE. A. letter dated 25th July, was read before this com- mittee from Me3.TB Peace and Ellis, enclosing a draft agreement from Messrs Housemen and Company, Lerd Newton's flo icitors, with reference to the proposed new 1 road from Craw-lane to Wargrave and the laying of gag mains therein. It was resolved that the terms of thel 'agreement be approved, and that the Chairman of the Council, with Mr. Beatty and the Clerk, wait upon the 1 Rev. Father Lennon to arrange terms for an additional four feet of land on the east side of the proposed read immediately at its cernmencement in Crow-lane. It was ordered that the Surveyor prepare for the next meeting alternate estimates for a cart bridge over Sankey Brook. below Vitriol Square. and necessary alterations to the road leading from Bra.dlegla-road to the said bridge, and for a footbridtre only over the brook referred to ; also estimates for the flagging of north side of Wareravr-road from Brookfield-street to the junction of the proposed new road. It was resolved that the Clerk give notice to the owner of the van seized for non- payment of market tolls, stating that unless the amount of toll due, and all expenses be paid within seven daye from the date thereof ,legal proceedings be taken against him without further notice. Two letters, dated the 8 h and 10.;ta of Augult, were read from ten reaidents in the neighbourhood of Oxford-street, and Mrs Gauge of Market-street, respectively, again calling the attention of the Council to the huts on the nearke'eand the nuis- ance arising therefrom, owing to the same being infested with rats. The Surveyor also read his report of the same as to raising them at least 10 inches from the ground by wooden supports at the ends, the beck ant front to be open underneath for cleansing purposes, which was ap- proved of. The Clerk read letters dated August Bth and 13th, from Mr. A. C. Leslie, Lord Newton's agent, with reference to backing up of the partially completed Newton Brook sewer and his reply thereto, after con- sideration of which it was resolved that the Surveyor forthwith disconnect the said sewer. A letter, dated the 18th August. was read from Messrs. Peace and Ellie, solicitors, Wigan, with reference to the propoeed devia- tion of the line of sewer from Mill-lane to central sewage works, statine that the matter was still in the hands if Messrs, Housemen and Co., Lord Newton's solicitors. A letter dated the 18th August was read from the Clerk to the Gelborne Urban District Council, asking this Council to join them in the cat of repairing and point- ing the peraoetwalls at the Hollows culvert (Rob Lane.) It was Ito3llVed that the application be acceded to. The Sanitary Inspector's monthly report was read arising out of which it was resolved that the matter of John Sinfield, late a labourer in the Highways Department,for absconding with toll tickets and money he had collected for tolls at Newton Horse Fair on the 13th August, 1900. 1 be placed in the hands of the police, with iustructione, to trace his whereabouts and to prosecute him ; that the slaughter-houses reported on as insanitary, viz :—Mr R Jones, Hand and Banner Yard, Neween-te. Willows. Eerlestown Industrial Co-operative Society rear of 23, Earle-street, George Wild, roar of 59 Lees, street. Earleetewn: b° closed as from 29'7,h September, and that Ph slaughter-house teloneing to the Council) situate off Cross-lane, Etrleetown, be declared a public Slaughter-house as from the 29th September. It was resolved that a night foreman be advertised for for the Sanitary Department, at a wage of 273, per week; that another horse aril cart be purchased ; that Mr Woods of Wizen, veterinary surgeon, be authorised to purchaso a horse for the Council at not exceeding £5O ; and Chet tenders be invited for a suitable cart. The.minutes were approved on the proposition of the chairman.

GENER AL PURPOSE CO AMITTEEs A letter. elatei the 28th Joly, was read from Messrs. F. J. Leslie *rad Co.. Liverpool, Solicitors to the South Laneashi re Electric Supply Co., Limited, acknowledging the receipt of the Clerk's letter, in which it was stated that the Council had decided to oppose the application of the Company for a provisional order under the Electric Lighting Acts, and stated that they hoped the Council would give the representatives of the Company an interview, so that they might lay the nature of their proposals before them, whereupon it was resolved that the Clerk arrange for an interview with the Company and this Committee at these offices. The Chairman moved and Mr. Borren seconded the adoption of the minutes which were agrrse 1 t'. TESTIMONIAL TO MR. SHIRLEY. The Chairman moved a resolution that a testimonial be giv-sn to Mr. W. W. Shirley, on resigning his position as Clerk to the Council. Mr. Ormand seconded, and it was agreed to. Toe test of the testimonial is as follows :—" Having tendered to us your resignation as Clerk to the Urban District Counnil of Newton-in-Makerfield, which we re• ceived with very sincere regret, we desire, and feel it to be our duty, to furnish you with a testimonial as to the manner in which you have discharged the duties of the office during the period (sow nearly five years) you have occupied the position. We can speak of your great abil•- ties as a public official in the highest terms and and it is a pleasure to state that you have, from time to time been commended by the Local Govrument H iard district auditor for the very able and creditable way in which your accounts have been kept, and that during your tenure of the office there has not been a single surcharge. The correspondence of the Council, both upon legal and other matter4,has hen conducted with courtesy.general god sense, and discrimination. The miptes of the Council have been drafted and recorded in a manner which has Riven satisfaction to every member of the Council. We have at all times found you to be a man of high character and sterling integrity, and one in whom implicit con- fidence may be placed and be relied upon to carry out aria instructions which the Council or any Committee may authorise. Under all circumstances we have found you to be courteous, honest, steady and attentive to business, and we sincerely hone you may be successful in your new undertaking. Given under the common seal of the Urban District Council ef Newton-in-Maker-

div.head: Increased Drunkenness—Fewer Licences.
div.p: Increased Drunkenness—Fewer Licences.

The general licensing sessions for tbe borough of St. Helens was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday. The Mayor (Councillor Bsecham) presidel,beine accompanied by Sir David Gamble, Bart., Colneel W. W. Pilkington, Colonel R. Pilkington, M.P., Aldermen J. C. Gamble, A. Sinclair, T. Cook, and J. Massey ; Councillors T. R. Dixon Nuttall, J. Burchall. H. Martin, J. B. Leach, Colonel J. W. M‘Tear, Dr. Gaskell, Messrs. J. Cotton, T. Glover, and R. A. Pilkington. Chief Censcable Wool, in his annual report, stated that there had been 267 persons summoned for drunken- ness during the year, against 301. last year ; 655 had been apprehended for drunkenness, against 582, a total increase of 38. Two publicans had been proceeded against and one convicted. There are 146 puolic-houees and 129 beerhouses (last year 131) in the borough, with 10 grocers licences. Theestineeted population is 88,480, and the number of public and beerhouses 275, giving 321. persons to each of these licences. Two beerhouse licences have beea allowed to lapse since last year. The licensee who was convict d was /inn Burrows, of the Railway Inn, Worslev-brow. Sutton, who on January sth was fined 40s and 40e 6 1 costs for selling beer to a drunken person. The following notices had born given by persons who would apply for licences :—Allred Griffin, secretary to the St. Helens Cafe and Recreation Company, Limited, for billiard licences for the Central Cafe, Bridee-street,ani the Market Tavern a3C,13. ronns, 18, Market Place ; Hiram Lewnds, 27. War I-street, for a wine and spirit off licence for 16. Church-street, St. Helens ; Gervasa Strinrtellow, for a beer, wine, and spirit off licence for 1 and 3, Ormkirk-etreet. Referring to the resolution of the magistrates, passed in 1.897, with reference to children under thirteen years of age being served or being Riven sweets, &c., during the year he bad only had one report of a licensee having contravened this resolutien. He gave the licensee notice that the matter would be reported to the bench. The Mayor asked for the name of the liceneee who was reported for supplying children. Chief Constib'e Wood : &lea Heslarn. of the Locomo- tive Inn, Eilamsbridge-road, Sutton. Her servant sup- plied a boy aged seven with 31 worth of whl9kee The Mayor asked if Peter Cunliff e, off beerhouse licensee, of Chester-street, had resided on his premises throughout the year. Inspector Steel said he believed he had. The Mayor said that last year the Mayor made some strong remarks with reference to the number of people proceeded against for drunkenness, and the small num- ber of proceedings and convictions against publicises for permitting druneennoss, Tili3 year there was an increase of forty class of drunkenness, and there was only one cenvictien for permittine drank nresiss. The magistrates theught that that was not a rfght state of things, and better vigilance ought to be exercised by the police. The Bench were of opinion that a great deal more attention ought to be paid to the manner in which the licensed houses were conducted. The Mayor said all licences weuld be renewed except those of Ann Burrows, li. F. Stringfellow, Ellen Haslam and Peter Cunliffe, which would be deferred to the adjourned licensing day. The adjoierned Bete...ions will be held on Thursday September 27h. The following apolicatione were made :—Music licences : Georee Theiniss Rioley, White Hart, Chu:ch- street ; Charles Green, Rifle Corps, Duke-street ; Charles Carey, Y. M.C. 1., Duke-street ; Vslentine rilatior Arms, Sutton-road ; Jobs, Ritchie, Finger- post, Pa k-road ; John Thomas Fletch , Railway, Hotel, Shaw street ; and <Teter' Makin, Vulcan Peckers Hill-road. Music eased dancing licences Helens Industrial Co-operative Secietv, Baldwin-street E I ward Dolan, Voluisteer ; Them IS B oardman, People's Palace; Henry Rebels Sharp-street, James Drake, Town Hall ; William Collins, Herdshave- street. Billiard Licences : William King, Coc se. rooms, Mill-plane ; Alfred Griffin, Central Cafe, Bridge-street ; Alfred Gsitlia, Market Tavern Cocoa-rooms, Market- place. In answer to the bench, Chief Constable Wood said he left the iquesticre of granting music licences to the migistrar.ea. He failed to see where magistrates had in days past drawn the line. His feeline was that no licences were necessary or that ev -Ty public house should be granted a music licence. Teere were only a few liceeces granted, and be these rht it wae, calculated to draw people to a few houses to the deteiment of adjoin- ing houses. - - - .

Sir David Gamble: You are of opinion that licences have been granted to rooms that are no better than tho3o at th 3 Rifl, Corps Inn. Chief Ginstable Wood : Yes, sir. The bench retired for some time, and on their return the Mayor said that the music and dancing licnaces and billiard Ucences would be granted.bm with regard to the applications for mu3ic licences for pilhliohouses. the bench had passed the following rrsolution :—" That the applications for the renewal of music licences to the White Hart, the Fiuvr-ooSt, and Railw..y Hotel, be not granted, and alTo that no new music licNices be public houses (including the Rttl3 Corps) be granted, so that all public houses be on the same footing with regard to music licences ; tbe magistrates not considering it de- sirable that public houses should h. music saloons.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN• [BY A CORTINRPONDENT.]
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN• [BY A CORTINRPONDENT.]
CRICKET.

The fag end of the season witnesses the worst parformance by Earlestown for some time past. They played their return fixture with StAlelens on the latter's ground, and although a draw was the result, still the game was in such a position that ba lit been played out there was very small chance indeed of EirieS own securing victory. St. Helens closed their innings for the 104 s of only 4 wickets, but Narlestown had notapprlached their score with eight wickets down. Doubtless the fact that the season had waned had some bearing on the play.

Newton had a very pleasant out on Saturday to Llandudno, to play the team of that very popular seaside resort. They were to goo'', however, for the Llandudno team, as for the lose of only seven wickets they had scored 86, as against Llandudno 82, all out.
FOOTB ALL.

The Socker game is now in full swing at Earles- town, and on Saturday the local representatives opened with a League fixture with Staleybridge R3vers. The home eleven had great expectations and they certainly should have won, but as usual, the luck was all against them. The new forward, Bartley, had stripped for play, but the Staleybridge officials recognised in him, one of the players of two seasons ago, and knowing that he had not been formally transferred, they objected to him taking part in the game. There was no help for it, and for some considerable portion of the first half of the game, Earlestown had to play with only ten men. The game was evenly contested during the first half, rind at half time there had been no score. Staleybridge had a penalty awarded them, but they were unable to gat the ball past Coew. Tee game ended, however, in Staleybridgo securing victory by 2 goals to nil.

The absence of Bartley from the team no iloubt made all the difference, although .Nloran, another new player, worked very hard alone, until he was joined by Linton. Clibborn at half back was a stumbling block in the path of the opposing for- wards and he many times staved off disaster. The transfer of Bartley has now lommi completed, and he will play tc-morrow in the home match against Darwen.
Newton who have joined the Cloabinatinn, had to iourney to Buckley to play the Balkh-5y Victorians, but they had to return home deteated by 4 goals to 1.

The Earle-town Rver, tnet Whiston on the latter' ground in the Liverpool and District A mlxteur Lague and as they secured the victory very easily by 4 goals to 1, it would appear as if they intended repeating their performance of last season and going through almost unbeaten.

THE GUARDIANS OF THE POOR OF TIER RUNCORN UNION are desirous of receiving TENDERS from parties willing to CONTRACT for the supply of FLOUR. OATMEAL, GROCERIES, PEAS. CHEESE SALT BUTTER ' - COD LIVER and PARAFFIN OIL; QUININE ; GOOD BEEF, to consist of vein pieces intact and Flat Ribs with Bone. one soun(l weekly not to exceed 251b5., and per week of the Best Butcher's Meat for the Officers, and Sides of Mutton • BREAD. HOME-CURED BACON. POTATOES. WHEAT'. STRAW. DRAPERY, and CLOTHING ; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' SHOES of various sizes, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse. Dutton, and Shoe Mending; HOUSE COAL ;Colliery to be named) ; GOOD DEAL COFFINS, specifying size. and Including plate with name, age, an t date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; COKE ; CARTING at per mile; FUNERALS at per Funeral. Parties Tendering for the supply of the above-mentionel Goods will be required todeliver the same at the Workhouse. free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except Drapery Goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any Tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Runcorn, tor a printed Form of Tender (and none other can he entertained), where a Schedule of the various articles required and further particulars may be obtained. Staled Tenders addreased to the Guardians, to be for- warded to the Clerk's Office, Runcorn, on or before Saturday the 22nd day of September. 1900, endorsed" Tender for The Tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 25th day of September. 1933, at 12-45 p.m. Parties whose Tenders are accepted must enter into a written Contract. and be prepared to enter into a Bond with two sureties if required by the Guardians. By Order of the Board. GEO. F. A.SHTON. Clerk to the Guardians. Runcorn, lst September, 1900.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. DISEASES OF ANIMALS ACT, 1894. FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on Friday, the 31st day of August, 1900, IT WAS ORDERED that from and after the Ist day of September MO, the movement of Animals (i e., CATTLE, SHEEP GOATS, AND ALL OTHER RUMINATING ANIMALS AND SWINE) Into the District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester from the Counties of DENBIGH- SHIRE and FLINTSHIRE, and from the District of any separate Local Autboritv situate within either of such Cuunties respectively BE ABSOLUTELY PROaIBITED REGINALD PO rrs, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 31st August, 1900. --- NOTE. The District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester does not includeS the City of Chester, nor any of the Municipal Boroughs situate therein. Animals shall not be deemed to be moved into the District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester trom the Counties of Denbighshire and Flintshire, where they are moved through such district or any part thereof by railway without unnecessary delay, and without the animals being untrucked or rcbooksd within such district or any part thereof. Animals cannot be moved into the County of Chester that may have been at any time during the continuance of the foregoing Regulations within the crohibited Counties of Denbighshire and Flintshire Any offence against the above Regulations is deemed an offence aeainat the Diseases of Animals Act, 1894, Which renders the offender liable to the penalties therein provided.
